items.title: Yaga Episode 7 and 8 Recap and Review
items.author: Jessie Wade
items.content:
Warning: This review contains full spoilers for Season 1, episodes 7 and 8. The full season is now streaming on AMC+ in the US and Crave in Canada.

The first part of the two-episode finale of Yaga opens with the Baba Yaga narrator saying, “it always has to be three…” as we see Rapp wandering in the woods at the ritual space. He looks down, puzzled, to see a red cooler on the ground with fish inside, and within that a ceramic jar made by Olena (Laney, as we know her) – and the jar has testicles in it. He blinks, and is still holding the jar and has the cooler, but is standing out on the dock near Carson’s boat at the marina.

We see Henry’s parents for the first time at the coroners, where they are looking at Henry’s body. We find out Henry was brutally murdered one week ago, with chicken feathers shoved down his throat before being burned alive. The pathologist, Jake, confirms he was castrated prior to death, as well.

As Rapp tells Henry’s mother, Dora, that he disagrees with Geena having been the one to murder him – he shares his own clues we’ve seen him gather over the past few episodes regarding Baba Yaga – and it’s clear that everyone in the room thinks he’s crazy. Dora tells him sternly that he had one job to do, and that was to protect Henry – and she fires him on the spot. As she walks away, Rapp tells her, “I know where all your bodies are buried.” Yet, Dora does not seem concerned about the threat.

Carson confronts Eckert about Geena previously sharing how he threatened and physically assaulted her – he only denies it, all while trying to make Carson feel guilty for even thinking something so awful of him. A lovely icing on the cake for someone who seems to be trying to cover their tracks while using manipulation tactics.

We see that Rapp has snuck up into Olena’s room at the hospital to try and pull more information out of her regarding Baba Yaga, as he believes, based on his discoveries, there will be a third murder following Logan and Henry’s. As usual, Olena is being evasive and cheeky, until Rapp pulls out her journal. For the first time, we see her looking legitimately concerned about this being in his hands, as he begins speaking the words written down in Ukrainian.

Olena starts to work with him on this for reasons unknown, and Rapp guesses that not only are there three murders planned, but there are three Yagas. Olena responds with, “Three to live forever,” as Rapp starts to put the puzzle pieces together – the third and youngest Yaga needs to have a baby to continue the cycle.

Right when we think Olena might actually reveal who the youngest Yaga is, she tells Rapp a sacrifice is needed before she divulges that the sacrifice is a kiss for her. All that’s needed is one kiss, but Rapp ends up becoming entranced and begins making out with Olena as he sees flashes of her as a young woman on the bed, surrounded by flowers. She ends up saying the third Yaga is “onuka,” which translates to “granddaughter” – confirming she herself must be the oldest Yaga, but it’s unclear who her granddaughter is. She takes off her top and right as he’s going further with her, Katherine barges into the room and yells, “What are you doing to my mother?!”

Rapp, shocked that Katherine is Olena’s daughter and convinced she is connected to the murders, begs Carson to go with him to Katherine’s house to try and get any other morsel of intel. As they’re sitting at Katherine’s dining table, discussing this (calmly at first), Rapp drops his conclusion, saying, “I think you, your mother, and your daughter are a multigenerational team of serial killers who think they are witches, who are punishing bad men for hurting women.”

“I don’t buy your act. I am ancient, you stupid little boy.”

Katherine looks unimpressed, saying, “Well that sounds fucking fantastic.” As this is all happening, Carson looks to be slightly restless, fidgeting every so often while Rapp and Katherine argue through this all. After voices raise, arguments escalate, and Rapp accuses Katherine of murdering Henry and lying about it, Katherine kicks them out of her house. While they are leaving, she also puts Rapp in his place, reminding him that every time he came on to her, he had an ulterior motive. She says to him, “I don’t buy your act. I am ancient, you stupid little boy,” and the line is delivered brilliantly.

Rapp is continuing to try and convince Carson he is correct with his theory, and explaining the pattern of “333” that he’s seen basically everywhere during his time in Whittock. He believes the third victim will be killed the following morning on March 3rd at 3:33am. Before Carson heads to meet with Dora, who has requested a private meeting with her at an upscale bar, she begs Rapp to wait in his hotel room for her until she figures out the next steps they should take. He eventually gives in, and she kisses him goodbye, hoping he will trust her on this.

Immediately, the meeting with Dora seems to have an underlying tone of danger to Carson, as Dora blames Henry’s horrific behavior on his father, saying he came after both her and Alice (Logan’s mother) when they were young – it is unclear if it was consensual or not. We get confirmation that Henry and Logan were in fact half brothers, which is more disturbing after knowing they previously had some type of infatuation with one another… and acted on it.

It’s starts to be pretty clear that Dora’s ulterior motive was wanting to keep the fact that Henry raped Lily under wraps. In turn, she offers a job to Carson “for life” working for the Parks. Carson politely declines, and Dora comments, “If you’re working for Eckert, you’re already working for us.” As this information sinks in, Dora unsurprisingly leaves her with a threat before walking away.

Rapp, continuing his hunt to find out who the third Yaga and killer is, sweet-talks his way into Pam’s apartment by means of her roommate. While there, he discovers the witch mask, along with Henry’s watch – and shockingly, that Pam is on a date with Eckert, making him potentially the next victim.

As we get to the end of the episode, Rapp calls Carson to fill her in on his findings, saying he’s heading to the woods and thinks he knows how to make Baba Yaga’s cabin magically appear. He tells her he needs her to meet him there – that he needs a partner. As she hesitantly agrees, she picks up Eckert as well, and we find out (disturbingly) that Eckert was in fact supposed to be on a date with Pam, but she stood him up. Along with that, Olena is missing from the hospital, and Katherine is not picking up her phone.

Episode 8 picks up right where Episode 7 ended, with Rapp in the woods searching for Baba Yaga’s cabin.

After prying, Eckert admits to Carson the truth of what he did to Geena and that he covered up Lily’s sexual assault – saying he did it for his kid. But Carson shows no sympathy. At this point, Rapp is already deep in the forest, speaking spells in Ukrainian and following a line of chickens to find Baba Yaga’s cabin. All of a sudden, he stumbles upon it, seeing warm lights glowing through the windows and someone inside the old, wooden hut.

As Rapp peers through the window, he sees bones hanging from the ceiling, and two women inside: Katherine and Olena – the former immediately looks towards him. He ducks away from the window, trying to hide. After a moment, Katherine is there with a knife at his throat, taking his gun away.

The two women lead him into the hut, where his view is distorted as they sit him down in a chair and Katherine tells him, “You’re just in time for the big show” as she ties his wrists together, all while Olena is holding the gun pointed at him, making jokes about it being a “good sword” and pretending to shoot him. Katherine also reminds Olena she is “at home” and not at the hospital – another interesting development, confirming our suspicions that they are the two elder Yagas.

The tight shots in the cabin mixed with the glowing embers of the fire in the small space really make you feel like you were pulled into that room with Rapp as well, witnessing all of the chaos unfold. Rapp begins to share his theory, which he’s extremely confident in: Pam is Katherine’s daughter, Anna, who is luring Eckert to the woods to have sex with him, and then will kill him at 3:33am. Katherine gives mock approval that he clearly knows everything that is to happen.

Carson and Eckert come upon the cabin, looking through the windows and seeing Rapp tied up inside. Despite Eckert saying he feels fucked up and wants to wait for backup, they burst into the cabin, guns drawn. Following shouting and Eckert demanding Olena lower her gun, Carson shockingly steps over to Olena and Katherine, grabs the gun from Olena, and shoots Eckert in the shoulder.

“I told you to leave it alone. I told you to wait for me at the motel,” Carson says as the camera slowly zooms in on her while she stares directly into Rapp’s eyes across the room. Within seconds, Olena refers to Carson as “Anna” and the shock and confusion on Rapp’s face increases threefold as he realizes who Carson really is.

She is Katherine’s daughter. She is Olena’s granddaughter. She is the third Yaga.

While we as viewers also take in this information, one’s mind goes into a frenzy thinking back on everything we saw with Carson – every little detail that we may have missed. In Episode 7, Katherine says to Carson as she’s leaving her house, “And officer, the last I checked, your job is justice for victims, not helping some billionaire fixer.” That line and so many others now have completely different meanings following this shocking reveal.

Carson knocks out Eckert, and the scene continues unfolding as Carson and Katherine argue about killing Eckert or killing Rapp. We hear Carson saying she wants to give more of the potion to Eckert, that she will have sex with him to get pregnant and have his baby, and will kill him instead of their apparent plan to do so with Rapp. Carson is then speaking in Ukrainian to Olena, trying to convince her of this new plan, saying that Eckert is a bad person and Rapp is much better than him, while Rapp is catching up to the fact that he is supposed to be the one who dies – the third man. The bad dog.

As he’s panicking, Carson tells him to shut up because she’s trying to help him. He says there must be a mistake. “Oh, no mistake,” Olena states simply, while Katherine adds, “No, no, you were chosen.” Rapp asks Carson if she knew, and she responds, looking almost defeated as she says, “not at first.”

As Rapp is grasping all of this in a panic, we find out even more revelations, including that the various young women in town (Olena’s “little witches”) were in on it and helped lay down the clues for Rapp to uncover, including the texts from Henry, the testicles in the cooler, and spiking Rapp’s drink earlier in the night while he was looking through Pam’s room.

And we finally get the answer we’ve been waiting for all along: Katherine killed Henry and Logan, which she proudly admits.

Carson continues arguing to save Rapp’s life and instead kill Eckert, saying that yes, Rapp is an asshole and a fuckboy, but he’s not a “bad dog.” In another shocking twist, Katherine’s response to that is to finally just shoot Eckert and kill him, leaving Carson screaming at her in response. Katherine says defensively that it wouldn’t have worked and they need to proceed as planned.

"Maybe I enjoy knowing these men will never hurt anyone ever again.”

In response to Carson asking Katherine why they have to kill them, Carrie-Anne Moss delivers her next line flawlessly, saying, “What, take them to court so they can throw the cases out? Henry raped a child. Logan did nothing. Maybe I enjoy knowing these men will never hurt anyone ever again.”

Rapp tells Carson that he loves her, and Katherine pulls Carson to look at her as she tells her, more seriously than ever, that he’s a liar and she herself knows it in her gut. “Yaga is the punisher. Bad dog is the invisible monster, and Yaga is the only one who can see him.” Katherine continues saying, “we are all Yaga, and if you don’t kill him, she ends with you. This is your birthright.”

Carson states that she wants her future daughter to have a choice in the matter, not being forced to be born from having a father who was a terrible person and who is dead. At this point, Rapp is desperately trying to convince them to release him by painting a picture of him helping them go after all the bad dogs, utilizing his years of experience working for the Parks and having dirt on many, many people.

Just when we think he might actually be safe, and Carson might refuse to go through with it all, Rapp tells her he has “the tape” of Henry raping Lily, saying they could use that against the Parks. Carson is immediately suspicious, asking why he has it without her knowledge. He says he took it to expose the truth of what happened. Right away, she knows he’s lying, and she says no – he took it as an insurance policy to protect himself. As this is happening, we see Rapp working at cutting the zip ties from his wrists behind the chair.

Carson looks directly at him and says, “I’m ready” and Katherine comes over to her as they prepare to start the ritual of torture. Rapp is now screaming and begging for them to stop, and right as Carson leans down, about to castrate him, he gets free and knocks her back as he flees out of the cabin.

We see Rapp running through the woods to a clearing on a cliffside near the beach, as Carson finds him – she keeps calm and acts like nothing happened, saying she just found him wandering in the woods. He’s shouting at her about how he knows she’s a witch, yet she’s pretending like she doesn’t know what he’s talking about.

Noah Reid’s acting throughout both of these episodes is phenomenal, especially in this scene, as he’s breaking down and saying he knows he’s a piece of shit, but he wants to be better. He shows his desperation, but also seems to possibly mean what he’s saying. He wants to be a good dog, not a bad dog. He’s sobbing and begging for forgiveness.

Right as he’s about to go to Carson and trust her, he sees Katherine walk up behind her, and he knows it’s a lie. He quickly calls for “The Horns” from a previous fairytale Katherine had shared on the podcast, where a phoenix will come and save a worthy opponent in this situation. He sees a phoenix come towards him in the sky and he jumps off the cliff towards it, despite both women telling him that’s not going to work. Unfortunately, the phoenix does not save him, and he is not freed from being the chosen one for the Yaga’s. He falls and smashes his head on the ground, but he’s still alive.

The next time we see Rapp is the last time, as he’s naked and tied to a tree while Carson lights a fire around him, burning him alive. The three Yagas are then grinding his bones in the mortar and pestle. The episode closes out with Carson telling the Parks what the final decision was on their case – which was, of course, fabricated to put others like Rapp at fault, and free Geena while also exposing what Henry did to Lily. The Parks are unsurprisingly shocked that they are not getting their way. Justice is served.

At the very end, after the screen fades to black, we see Carson having her baby, while speaking about there only being three Yagas at once to make room for the newborn. Olena is in the background and Katherine is holding the baby, and all of a sudden concern flashes across her face when Carson asks to see her – with Katherine responding, “It’s a boy.”

Carson seems shocked, but still looks to be nothing but enamored by her baby boy. From what we now know about this tale of Baba Yaga, there are only daughters, so it will be interesting to see what story develops next in Season 2.

items.title: Percy Jackson and the Olympians Season 3, Episodes 3 & 4 Recap and Review
items.author: Jacob Kienlen
items.content:
After a great season premiere to set up the show's new quest, Percy Jackson Season 3 dives straight into the action with Episodes 3 and 4. The Oracle's prophecy looms and death is in the air. The Greek mythology of it all is on full display as our heroes set out to save Annabeth, encountering ancient monsters and gods along the way. With four episodes down, the series is now firing on all cylinders.

Episode 3 kicks off right where Episode 2 left off. The Oracle has given the prophecy, the quest-goers have been chosen, and the mood is pretty somber. This is the first time in the series so far where we've seen the campers receive a quest that has the word "perish" right there. Artemis' Hunters and members of Camp Half-Blood were chosen to go on the quest, but Percy Jackson is noticeably absent from that list. Like every prophecy, however, the details are up to interpretation and Percy gets a surprising bit of help from Dionysus to bend the threads of fate and sneak him into the quest.

It takes Percy most of the episode to actually be reunited with the rest of the group, which means we get the chance to see Grover truly shine. Grover has been a part of two quests at this point and he knows exactly what to do. Even though he's with a daughter of Zeus and an elite Hunter of Artemis, he takes charge and gets everyone moving in the right direction. Whenever he pulls out that pan flute, you can trust him to find a way to hold everything together. And when he and Percy are finally reunited, he plays an essential role in evading the Spartoi and the taking on the Nemean lion.

And while Percy and Grover are the main drivers of the action in Episode 3, it's Bianca and Nico that bring the emotional depth. We watch Bianca (Olive Abercrombie) go from nervous protective sister to budding demigod warrior and can't help but root for her to succeed. Meanwhile, Nico (Levi Chrisopulos) pushes Percy to bring him along on the quest, showcasing his determination to help his sister. The di Angelo siblings' character development in this episode feels substantial, and it arrives just in time for the biggest tragedy of The Titan's Curse.

Episode 4 is Percy Jackson and the Olympians at its very best. The heroes are on the run from the relentless Spartoi and Nico is forced to part from his sister once again. But not before he makes Percy promise to protect her. This is a pivotal moment in the story, and Walker Scobell does an excellent job of portraying Percy's hesitation to make such a promise. He knows that at least one person is prophesied to perish on this quest, but he has this kid in front of him looking to put his faith in a hero, rather than a god. This promise adds to the weight Percy is already carrying, and things only get heavier for him from here on out.

The characters don't have much time to ponder the larger threads of fate as the Spartoi force the story forward with their relentless march

After escaping the Spartoi (for now), Percy and crew have their first run-in with the gods. Ares is waiting outside a car with obvious hostile intent, which is only intensified by Thalia and Percy taking an equally aggressive stance to the meeting. But thankfully the God of War is only there on behalf of his lover, Aphrodite (Kate McKinnon). She reveals that not only are the gods planning a vote on whether or not to go to war, they will also be voting on whether or not to kill Percy and Thalia. It's their fear that one of the kids will slay the Bane of Olympus and fulfill the great prophecy, but Aphrodite says her vote is for Percy and the power of love. She then gives him the key to her husband's (Hephaestus) junkyard as a boon to help him on his quest.

Their encounter with Aphrodite is a good bit of storybuilding, unravelling just the right amount of the greater prophecy that haunts Olympus. It also sets Thalia down that same path of fear, working to convince Percy that it's now a kill or be killed situation they find themselves in. But the characters don't have much time to ponder the larger threads of fate as the Spartoi force the story forward with their relentless march. This all sets the stage for the reveal of the Junkyard of the Gods, which is a sight to behold.

As you might expect, the Junkyard of the Gods is a massive collection of legendary scrap. Huge piles of rusty metal tower into the sky and the atmosphere has an otherworldly orange desert hue. They may have escaped the Spartoi, but now they are somhwhere that feels dangerous on an entirely different level. It's out of the frying pan and into the fire as Percy and his friends accidentally activate a giant defense robot and find themselves having to split up. At this point, things are getting really serious and tensions are running extremely high.

Like any epic tale, impossible moments like these are what give heroes the opportunity to heroes. While everyone is split into separate groups, Percy has found himself conveniently in a position where he can still hear everyone else, even if they can't hear him. And what he hears is the same fear that is plaguing Olympus, only it's creeping into the hearts of his companions. As the enormous robot stomps closer, he feels that same fear reaching him. It's only through a fortunate encounter with Tyson (via a magical call) that he is able to come up with a plan and shake that fear.

Bianca's character arc reaches its crescendo as fate puts her in a pivotal position to save everyone, and she leaps at the opportunity.

With a plan in motion, Percy does what he does best and gives a rousing (if somewhat cheesy) speech to the group. Morale is lifted, fear is banished, and the group heads out to shut down the giant automaton currently hunting them. With everyone now working together, Percy is able to successfully reach the entry hatch located in the robot's heel. But he can't open it alone, and the one person he's sworn to protect is the only one that can help him get it open. Bianca's character arc reaches its crescendo as fate puts her in a pivotal position to save everyone, and she leaps at the opportunity.

Fate isn't kind, though. The now lifeless automaton tumbles to the ground with Bianca still inside, fatally wounding her in the process, and fulfilling the second part of the Oracle's prophecy: "One shall be lost in the land without rain." It's a devastating loss. Up until this point, Percy and his friends have made it out unscathed. Now Percy has suffered a massive loss and broken his promise to Nico. He's facing life or death consequences and nothing will ever be the same again after this. This moment is one of the darkest turning points in the entire Percy Jackson series, signalling even more death is on the horizon.

items.title: South Park Season 29 Finale Review: 'City Endings'
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
There hasn't been a real, concerted effort to build an overarching narrative in South Park Season 29. Sure, certain plot threads have carried forward, like the arrival of Little Randy and Kenny's latest brush with death, but by and large this season has just drifted from one topic to the next. But that doesn't stop Trey Parker, Matt Stone, and the rest from trying to tie everything together in the finale. It's a pretty messy conclusion - a City Ending, even - but a mostly entertaining one.

As was teased throughout this season, everything culminates with November's big event. Not the US midterms, but the long-awaited arrival of GTA 6. Literally everyone in town is busy playing Rockstar's masterpiece, which makes things kind of awkward when it turns out the majority of South America's power grid is being hijacked by billionaire weenies and their data centers.

I definitely would have preferred a more focused and organic approach to weaving together this season's various storylines, but I do appreciate the effort to tie it all together here at the end. "City Endings" does a pretty good job of lampooning all the AI-related headlines that have swirled as of late, from the Jensen Huang/AMD situation to the recent spate of technical meltdowns. It's especially fitting that we see the characters collectively lose their minds over imagined Chinese cyberattacks rather than look inward and realize the problem is coming from inside the house.

It doesn't hurt that the show swings back around to focus on Mr. Kim and the latest evolution of City Wok, which has now been transformed from a clearing house for crappy e-bikes to a sordid massage parlor. It's pretty amusing to watch Kim frantically run around trying to "please" his growing lineup of customers while his disinterested wife goofs off in the back. I complain a lot about the series regurgitating the same jokes over and over, but here I think there's a nice sense of escalation over the course of the episode. I'll also be curious to see if the ending holds and whether Kim returns from his little sojourn in space.

"City Endings" also makes solid use of Butters and his family, as we see how thoroughly corrupted Butters has become thanks to his proximity to power and wealth. We get a fun little parody of The Twilight Zone episode "It's a Good Life," at least until Butters is exposed. That's a great way of paying off on the whole antivax subplot from earlier in the season. There's even a hilariously sad little bit involving Peter and his hapless attempt to insert himself into the Kenny-shaped hole in the group.

Again, this episode is nothing if not chaotic in its attempts to weave all of Season 29's ongoing threads together. There are certain things I would have liked to see more payoff for, including the Little Randy of it all (is this just the ongoing status quo for that character now?). I also felt the Kenny subplot deserved a little more focus than it receives here. But despite those concerns, "City Endings" works as a largely satisfying conclusion to a very uneven season of South Park. And now we don't have to refer to the show as "South America" any longer.

items.title: We Build LEGO Godzilla, Who Will Tower Over Your Other LEGO Models
items.author: Chris Reed
items.content:
This is a bulky build that looks more impressive in person than it does on its box cover. It comes with two interchangeable mouth insertions: either a large tongue or an Atomic Heat Ray, the latter of which extends his height to over two feet tall. Space concerns aside, the choice seems clear if you're putting this city stomper on display.

Godzilla fans should know this model is based upon the ongoing 'Monsterverse' iteration of the creature, which began with Godzilla(2014). Monsterverse is an American franchise, not to be confused with the original Japanese Toho franchise, which released its 34th film (Godzilla Minus Zero) this November.

But artists have redesigned Godzilla many times, including from movie to movie. So even though it might not be the exact Godzilla you love the most, this LEGO model is immediately recognizable as the icon, because it has the general characteristics that most iterations share in common: the pear-shaped body, the comparatively smaller dinosaur head, and the dorsal fins that line its back. The model's main inspiration is the Godzilla from Godzilla: King of the Monsters (2019), but even so, it's a bit sleeker and thinner than that one. So it might be best to think about this as yet another monster design alongside the others – loyal to the design ethos, but unique in its approach.

LEGO Godzilla comes in a large box, which encases two smaller boxes. Each smaller box contains approximately 20 bags. Added together, it's 41 bags in all, plus three instruction booklets. There are no stickers and no printed tiles.

You build one leg, then the pelvis, and then the other leg. You connect both legs to the pelvis with durable ball joints, and stand it up. To give you an idea of how bottom-heavy Godzilla is: Just the legs and pelvis comprise half of the entire build. And even so, LEGO made clever design choices to accentuate his bulk. Take the armor plating on his lower legs, for example. They hang off a hinge near the ankle, which creates the illusion of a thicker, more substantial leg, even though it's mostly air with no bricks to fill it out.

Then you focus on the tail, which you build in segments. Connecting them all creates a sense of accomplishment, because most large LEGO builds (including this one) take shape through layering, first by building the Technic skeleton underneath and then building the musculature and skin via plating. But with the tail, you're seeing the entire appendage take form in front of you, immediately, and it's easy to see where it begins and where it will eventually end.

Each tail segment contains dorsal fin elements. You need to either build directly onto the tail piece or clip a larger fin to it, which adds a varied, visual touch. The tail drags along the ground, and the instructions let you decide whether it will rest on the left side or the right side of the creature. You then turn to the correct page (sort of like a Choose-Your-Own-Adventure book) and proceed.

The third and final instruction booklet shows you how to build the arms, the head, and some final, large dorsal fins on the creature's back. These are the fussiest parts of the build, owing to their smaller size and weaker connection points. But when everything is complete, the final result is very intimidating. Ironically, the smaller head and arms only emphasize how large the rest of the creature is. Godzilla's skin cleverly appropriates the LEGO bricks' pips as rough texture.

This is a wonderful model, and we recommend it with one important reservation; it is best displayed from a side profile angle only, with its head pointed upwards. Any other angle or posture, and the model looks odd and ungainly.

I think the reason for this one-dimensionality – for favoring one possible display angle over the others – is the developers were trying to nail a single, iconic Godzilla pose. It's this one from the promotional poster for Godzilla: King of the Monsters, in which Godzilla is looking up, shooting his atomic heat ray directly towards the heavens:

And to be fair, this model nails that pose very, very well, and it looks exactly like the poster. But that comes at the sacrifice of other possible poses. Take the neck, for example. To ensure that the head can tilt up convincingly, the designers included extra grey bricks around the neck to hide the seams. That's a great thing, but only for that specific pose. Those extra bricks limit Godzilla's movement, and he can only point his head up, diagonally up, or straight across. He can't, for example, look down, which is a problem if you want to pose him looking down at the city or humans he's about to destroy.

It's not a problem isolated to the neck either; the back is also ramrod straight and does not allow Godzilla to adjust himself down or forward. Again, that's fantastic . But it doesn't serve Godzilla well for any other, alternative setup.

Normally, this sort of one-notedness, especially in adult sets, wouldn't be that big of a deal, because an adult set doesn't need to be a malleable plaything. But because so much of our popular concept of Godzilla has him looking down at things rather than up at them, it's especially noticeable.

Surely, a creative builder can modify the current set for more flexibility. And then, LEGO Godzilla can look down as he stomps some LEGO Ninjago cities, while minifigures scream and scramble for dear life.

LEGO Godzilla (Set #21375) retails for $449.99 and includes 5363 pieces. It will be available beginning on Black Friday, November 27.

items.title: Tangles Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
Tangles is in theaters in New York and Los Angeles on Nov. 27. It will expand to a wider release in January.

The weight of memory is vital to the biographical animated feature Tangles, a black-and-white story about family, the queer ‘90s, and above all else, early-onset Alzheimer’s. Based on the sparse but powerful by Sarah Leavitt — who co-wrote the screenplay with Trev Renney and director Leah Nelson — the film employs abstractions in its margins and connective tissue, making room for straightforward drama that proves incredibly moving in its unearthing of lived experience.

Beginning with a childhood flashback, Tangles introduces us to middle-aged Midge (Julia Louis-Dreyfus), based on Leavitt’s mother, as she helps a young Sarah (Fern Grandin) fight invisible monsters in her bedroom, with the help of a flashlight which Sarah imagines as a fuchsia lightsaber. Midge is, for all intents and purposes, Sarah’s superhero, but life goes on as the film skips forward to 1999. The adult Sarah, voiced by Abbi Jacobson, draws for a queer magazine in San Francisco, but a return to her hometown for a family visit proves a major turning point. Everyone including Sarah’s soft-spoken father Rob (Bryan Cranston), her idiosyncratic aunts Debbie (Pamela Adlon) and Sukey (Sarah Silverman) and her lively sister Hannah (Beanie Feldstein) seems to dance around major changes in Midge’s lifestyle and cognitive function.

They blame it, at first, on menopause, and then on Midge losing her job and her ensuing depression, but minor tasks prove frustrating and confusing for the usually gentle 50-something, who’s drawn with appropriately haggard squiggles. It takes a while before a real diagnosis tells them what might be wrong: an early form of dementia. This forces Sarah to fly back and forth between her family and her supportive, stud girlfriend Donimo (Samira Wiley), a schism of time, place and culture that slowly wears on her as Midge’s disease advances.

The dynamic between Sarah’s queer, urban environment and her nominally accepting but high-strung Jewish family allows the film to traverse different modes of expression and conversational rhythm, as she tries to be in two places at once. This dichotomy also helps enhance periods of nerve-wracking transition during lengthy travel, expressed through tongue-in-cheek formal flourishes. Each flight, for instance, becomes the venue for dreamlike jokes about Sarah’s deep-seated anxieties delivered over the plane’s PA system, leaving her vulnerable and exposed.

Louis-Dreyfus delivers a heartrending, piercingly realistic vocal performance as a woman trying to hold on to what little of herself she can find.

Sarah is a character perpetually on edge, a baseline made all the more volatile when she takes it upon herself to recognize her mother’s illness and care for her as best she can, even at the cost of her various relationships. Midge, meanwhile, slips away gradually over the film’s 102 minutes, as Louis-Dreyfus delivers a heartrending, piercingly realistic vocal performance as a woman trying to hold on to what little of herself she can find.

The period setting is rendered with appropriate details — a few too many Marvel references aside, it feels like a sketched memory of the late 1990s, from pop culture to the textures and technologies — but the story itself is timeless. Nelson brings Leavitt’s autobiographical tale to life with generosity, imbuing each supporting character with a palpable denial that feels, at first, like a mere quirk, before revealing itself to be a coping mechanism. The gradual confusion and anger involved (both for Midge and her caretakers) results in a moving portrait of helplessness in the face of a brutal disease, as well as the few moments of love people are able to steal from it while they still can. By the time the film wraps up, its echoes of Midge in earlier scenes continue to loom large thanks to Louis-Dreyfus’ fine-tuned performance as she leaves quiet gaps in her wake, alongside a sense of longing for the character she used to be.

items.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 Finale Recap and Review
items.author: Jim Vejvoda
items.content:
The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 finale, titled “The Doom of Men,” closes out a season that rejuvenated the flailing series with the promise that Sauron’s worst is yet to come in the just announced Season 4. For a season that was all about the One Ring and the anticipation of an epic battle between good and evil, “The Doom of Men” ends with Sauron proving that guile remains his most potent weapon against his adversaries.

The season’s penultimate episode (“Orodruin”) sees Sauron finally succeed in forging the One Ring with the aid of the Balrog (voiced by Simon Pegg). While it's intriguing to see the devil make a deal with another devil, Pegg's voice is so manipulated that any ol’ actor could’ve played him. Episode 7 also sees Míriel turn down Elendil and go through with marrying Pharazôn, thus uniting the Númenóreans. Meanwhile, Durin and his family are banished from Khazad-dûm but make off with one of the rings given to the Dwarf-lords. That’s the last we see of their storyline until next season as the Dwarves sit out the season finale.

“The Doom of Men” finally resolves the Gandalf/Dark Wizard storyline with sacrificing himself to save Gandalf in a classic ending in . Gandalf freed his old friend from the corrupting influence of the ring, which Pallando had apparently worn for all of an evening before Gandalf tricked him out of it. (Pallando wore the ring just long enough for the show to make an allusion to Gollum’s “my precious” line.)

While the wizards vs. Nazgnagôl battle feels awkwardly executed with all its obvious wire-work, at least it provides Gandalf and Pallando a few moments to finally fight side-by-side as allies. I’m not sure, though, if the Pallando storyline was ultimately worth taking up so much dramatic real estate over the last two seasons for such a brisk payoff. At the very least, Pallando’s death and the resulting liberation of his followers robbed Sauron of a good chunk of his army.

I enjoyed how Sauron tests Gandalf’s incorruptibility in a very Last Temptation of Christ manner, offering him the rule of Middle-earth if he’d just submit. I also liked Sauron’s short-lived ruse of conjuring a figment of Nori Brandyfoot (Markella Kavenagh in a cameo) in an attempt to dupe Gandalf, although I never believed that the show was in any real way.

Elrond evoking his brother to help instill some hope in the Númenórean soldiers on the eve of their likely deaths was a nice touch. Despite a moment where he allows himself to ask the advice of Galadriel and – whose relationship woes I haven’t found particularly interesting thus far – Pharazôn’s hubris ultimately gets the better of him. The Elves foresee the Doom of Men when Sauron surrenders, so I fully expect Season 4 to end with The Fall of Númenor.

items.title: Hexed Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
is in theaters on November 25.

Since the 100th anniversary of Disney Animation in 2023, The Walt Disney Company has released two feature animation sequels, (2024) and (2025), and two originals, (2023) and now Hexed. That’s certainly on brand with Disney’s current focus on making sequels to their hits, but not one of that pack rise to the level of game-changing for the historic animation studio. Though Hexed gets points for having an original story by Josie Trinidad (Zootopia+) and screenplay by studio CCO Jared Bush and Dana Ledoux Miller, it’s not conjuring for the fences with its less than fresh storytelling, typical computer-generated imagery, or CGI house style.

Directed by next generation Disney creatives Fawn Veerasunthorn (Wish) and Jason Hand (Moana 2), Hexed centers on rebellious 16-year-old Billie Doe (Hailee Steinfeld) and her helicopter mother Alice Doe (Rashida Jones). They live in the drabbest corner of Ohio where Alice has Billie on a tight leash regarding her every move, even when it comes to growing certain plants in her room (no, not plant). As revealed in the prologue, Billie was born with magical powers and their manifestation so freaked Alice out that she created a magic suppression bracelet Billie’s been required to wear ever since. The kind-authoritarian parenting approach has left Billie feeling like her mom hates her and goosed her rebellious side, resulting in an expulsion for freeing the school’s owl mascot.

Most importantly, Billie’s caper caused her bracelet to break, sparking up her long dormant powers and bringing forth a plant-based portal that drags her into the magical world of Hexe. This secret dimension was created by witches after the Salem witch trials and it’s filled with a cacophony of witches of all ages, animal Familiars, and Disney-fied hawkers that delight Billie and provide the basics on spell-casting – namely Intention, Ignition and Inwitchification. Playing around with her powers, Billie levitates and flies, which is only done by their ruler, Queen Celeste (Jodie Foster), and quickly gains the monarch’s attention and ire. But Type-A Alice is on the case and follows Billie to Hexe, revealing that she too is a witch and wants her daughter back in Ohio.

What ensues is an overly complicated quest which exposes that Hexe has been under the queen’s kind-authoritarian rule for years. She’s aggressively territorial about her power, so Billie and Alice are threats to her status quo and an impending spell ceremony that’s supposed to lock up her power base. Is it a surprise to find out that she’s got a deeper history with Alice too? Not really, but it explains why Alice fled her magical home when she was pregnant with Billie and has been in hiding ever since.

Hexed isn’t a bad film, but it’s underwhelming and doesn’t plant a flag of innovation animation-wise.

Hexed is firmly rooted in Disney’s corny and wholesome kind of comedy, drowning its audience in groaner dad jokes and bad puns like, “Witch, please.” Though Billie is classified a rebel, her only “sins” are stealing her mom’s car and calling something crappy once. She’s a good kid in the Disney princess way, and spends most of her road-tripping in Hexe bonding with Alice’s abandoned, three-eyed cat Familiar Beef Roger Crummchuk (Walton Goggins), an enchanted cast iron cauldron named Bucket and, eventually, her mom. Not exactly Violet from Arcane behavior (whom Steinfeld also voices), but maybe it's edgy for Disney-loving households.

Hexed can boast proudly about its sumptuous production design by Lorelay Bove, featuring rich colors and lighting that results in some arresting visuals and environments to look at during the trio’s travels. Goggins is also a standout and a hoot as the crusty cat Beef. However, the rest of the “original” aspects of Hexed are actually heavily borrowed from other films like Howl’s Moving Castle, Kubo and the Two Strings, Wicked, and many, many others. There’s even some purple palette swiping from the demon Saja Boys in KPop Demon Hunters. And interestingly, Hexed and the recent adaptation of share similar storylines about children gaining empathy for the sacrifices of their parents. However, the latter handles it in a far more interesting and emotional way than the heavy-handed approach Hexed takes with Billie, Alice and Celeste. All of it makes for a muddled story, with several sequences and characters that don’t make a lot of narrative sense in general.

As for the animation itself, Hexed has two sequences where the animators break from their CGI norms — a short, 2D shadow play prologue and then a dream state that’s rendered with a misty, brush-stroke overlay. Neither push what their animators can do stylistically or technically. They’re way too subtle, implying that Disney embrace stylization like the animators do at Dreamworks, Sony Animation and DNEG, who fully committed to mixing up their CGI animation years ago.

Sound-wise, beware that Hexed is a loud one. Much like DreamWork’s , this film embraces a cacophony of shouting characters and aggressive layers of environmental sounds along with quick cutting that’s meant to hold attention spans but is quite exhausting by the end. Add the astonishingly on-the-nose needle drops layered throughout, and Hexed could be accused of leaning far too much on aural tricks, rather than slowing down and trusting its own storytelling.

Hexed isn’t a bad film, but it’s underwhelming and doesn’t plant a flag of innovation animation-wise. Instead, it's just fine with being an attractive, broad comedy that probably won’t linger in audience minds much after the credits.

items.title: Focker-In-Law Review
items.author: Jim Vejvoda
items.content:
After 26 years and three films, Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro are back with another strained but silly installment in the Meet the Parents franchise. Focker-In-Law essentially retreads the premise of the 2000 film but this time with Stiller’s Greg Focker as the reluctant would-be father-in-law. It’s entirely predictable and formulaic but the players and the circumstances are just amiable enough to make it passably fun.

Greg (Stiller), his wife Pam (Teri Polo), and their adult twins Samantha (Beanie Feldstein) and Henry (Skyler Gisondo) converge on patriarch Jack Byrnes’ (De Niro) home to celebrate his 80th birthday. Samantha brings along her awkward but lovable boyfriend Eduardo (Eduardo Franco), while aspiring med student Henry introduces his folks to Olivia (Ariana Grande), the young woman he plans to pop the question to over the weekend. But in true Focker fashion, Greg has already soured things before he learns that the woman he had a bad encounter with on his flight was Henry’s girlfriend Olivia.

The weekend that follows sees Greg convinced that Olivia is, despite meeting with everyone else’s approval, up to no good. Greg repeatedly attempts to expose Olivia – a savvy former FBI hostage negotiator turned executive coach – which sees the two engage in a battle of wits the likes of which Greg has not faced since he first locked horns with Jack all those years ago.

As with the 2000 film, the combative premise pushes Greg into increasingly absurd and extreme antics while Olivia proves she’s sharp enough to remain neck-and-neck if not a step ahead of him throughout. Olivia isn’t related to Jack but she’s definitely his kindred spirit and game recognizes game. Played with a hefty dose of pluck by Grande, Olivia commands respect from men who otherwise underestimate her because of her looks or her small stature.

Grande acquits herself well here but the standout of the franchise’s new cast members is Skyler Gisondo as Henry, who lacks the nerve to establish boundaries with his infantilizing dad. The question of whether Olivia is manipulating Henry or has his best interests at heart is central to Greg’s single-minded mission to delay if not derail their engagement. Gisondo captures both the exasperation of having the likes of the well-meaning but perpetually ill-suited Greg Focker for a dad while never losing sight of the genuine affection he has for him.

Unfortunately, Beanie Feldstein isn’t really given much good material here as Samantha, who Greg has so coddled that she’s incapable of doing anything for herself. Her storyline is instead in service of her boyfriend Eduardo’s ambition to win a place in Jack’s Circle of Trust. Teri Polo is fairly marginalized with not much to accomplish in the story, while Blythe Danner barely registers as present as the Byrnes matriarch Dina. Faring a bit better is Owen Wilson, who reprises his recurring role as Pam’s wealthy ex, Kevin Rawley, who remains a beloved member of the Byrnes family much to Greg’s ongoing discomfort.

Turning 80, De Niro’s Jack has mellowed with age and is no longer as combative with Greg as he once was. Jack’s now on a health kick, which only gives vegan Olivia one more competitive advantage over Greg. De Niro seems to be having fun even if his delivery is mostly rote.

But this is Stiller’s movie and he continues to wring as much awkwardness as he can out of every rough situation of uncomfortable exchange Greg becomes ensnared in. So much of the humor and conflict in this movie is caused by Greg’s inability to ‘fess up to making a social faux pas and instead just digging the hole deeper for himself. The whole movie would be over in 10 minutes if Greg simply stopped to explain himself or ask for clarification.

items.title: Blade Runner 2099 Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
debut on Prime Video on November 25. This is a spoiler-free review.

There’s a scene in 2017’s where the very grim and serious Agent K (Ryan Gosling) makes a joke about a Wallace Corp. employee’s lost baby pictures. “Well, it’s a shame… you must’ve been adorable,” K says straight-faced. It’s a moment of levity in a pretty heavy movie, with Gosling playing it without even cracking a smile, and it works wonderfully to keep us afloat amid all the darkness – as do several other such instances in the film.

The people behind Blade Runner 2099, the latest installment in the series which began with the 1982 Ridley Scott/Harrison Ford movie, don’t understand this, or at the very least don’t think they need to include such moments of humor or lightness in their new show. As a result, watching Blade Runner 2099 very quickly turns into a slog, leading to an increasing feeling with each passing episode that the show is crushing inward on you like the teeming, downtrodden masses of its futuristic Los Angeles.

It’s not just the oh-so-serious scripting that leads to this unforced error, however. 2099 also suffers from the performances of leads Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer, who seem to be trying to out-gloom each other for most of these eight episodes. The result is a buddy-cop story where the cops not only aren’t buddies, but are also unappealing and ultimately a drag to be around. Where’s Harrison Ford and his noodles when you need them!?

Set 50 years after 2049 (obviously), and 80 years after Ford’s Deckard was Blading and Running, the new series picks up the threads of the Replicant revolution that was just about to get underway in that previous film. In the intervening decades, the Replicants – humanoid robots formerly used as slave labor, for those who have never actually seen a Blade Runner movie (and judging by box office figures, there are a lot of you) – won that war. So now, that which man made rules over man. And they’re not terribly nice about it, either!

It's a buddy-cop story where the cops not only aren’t buddies, but are also unappealing and ultimately a drag to be around. Where’s Harrison Ford and his noodles when you need them!?

Yeoh – who after the Star Trek disaster that was two years ago and now this misfire may want to reconsider the whole small screen sci-fi thing – stars as Olwen, a Replicant Blade Runner whose built-in termination date is nearing. She’s seen things you people wouldn’t believe, don’t you know, having lived Off-World in the past – something the franchise has only spoken about in previous iterations but never shown until now – but now she’s ready to head off to the great unknown like all Replicants must do…

Enter Schafer as Cora, a human who through a confluence of events winds up having to pretend to be a Replicant, and not just a Replicant, but a Replicant Blade Runner working among other Replicant Blade Runners. And those Replicant Blade Runners are smart! And wily! And dangerous! And as I said earlier, not terribly nice. It’s a tricky situation for Cora, and the constant look of paralyzed terror on her face is completely credible and understandable, given her situation. The only problem is that look becomes Schafer’s main mode for 2099, and when combined with Olwen’s icy shoot-first, put-a-weird-bag-over-your-head-that-shoves-a-tube-down-your-throat-later philosophy, the viewer may very quickly find themselves wondering who they’re rooting for here, or why.

Indeed, as the story progresses, involving the hunt for some mysterious information from deep in the Blade Runner past, there are a few supporting characters who are given a short time in the spotlight and actually prove that 2099 has inhabitants that are, you know, interesting. For example, this far into the future the Voight-Kampff machine – the device used to probe Replicants for empathy, or a lack thereof – has been replaced by human children who are seemingly sold by their parents into a life of indentured servitude and trained to be living empathy detectors. Katelyn Rose Downey plays one such child, a scary, inscrutable creature when we first meet her… until we get a bit of an origin story for her in a later episode. Then there’s Matthew Needham (Larys on House of the Dragon), who plays another Replicant who is smart, scary, and entirely dismissive of humanity. “Your whole world has already gone past you,” he says of mankind. Amy Lennox also appears as a Replicant, sort of cut from the Pris mode from the original film in that she’s child-like yet deadly. But most importantly, whenever she’s onscreen, it’s a reprieve from the constipated angst of our two leads.

And look, as a lifetime Blade Runner devotee – I saw the original film when it was first released in a drive-in with my parents! – I take no pleasure in dismissing 2099. I’m also fully aware that the whole thing about Blade Runner is being dark and dreary, with Ford’s Deckard complaining about his ex-wife (depending on which cut you watched) and Gosling’s K on a doomed mission of self-salvation and so on. Those guys weren’t exactly a barrel of laughs, but they did have a charisma that let their characters be part of the Blade Runner dystopia without being engulfed by it. That’s not the case here.

Which isn’t to say that 2099 doesn’t have its merits. Certainly the production is a wonder to behold – how they make these shows that look like big-budget movies these days and don’t break the bank is beyond me. This is the Los Angeles (and elsewhere) of Blade Runner, without a doubt, and every flying spinner car and Tyrell Corporation tower is perfectly realized. The costuming is, well, interesting at times, seemingly competing for the biggest shoulder pads in the history of shoulder pads, but hey, it’s the future!

And creator Silka Luisa (Shining Girls) and her staff make it clear that they understand the source material that they’re building on, not just in terms of the films but also the Philip K. Dick book on which it’s all based, Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? The trailers have already hinted at the inclusion of the book’s TV host Buster Friendly, but there are other aspects of the book that the show has time to touch upon which fans will appreciate. The fandom among the creative team is strong, but at times 2099 tries too hard to evoke the feel of the previous films, the 1982 original in particular. Ever wanted to see Rachael’s implanted memory of the spider outside her window? Well, you may be in luck here… or not, as the case may be.

items.title: Yaga Episode 6 Recap and Review
items.author: Jessie Wade
items.content:
Warning: This review contains full spoilers for Season 1, Episode 6. Episodes 1-6 are now streaming on AMC+ in the US and Crave in Canada, with new episodes releasing on Fridays at midnight PT.

Trigger warning: This review has references to sexual assault and non-consensual behavior depicted in the series.

Yaga Episode 6 dives into its deepest depths thus far, giving us answers that were left unknown from last week’s episode while revealing horrifying experiences in the town of Whittock.

Following Geena’s daughter, Lily, showing up at Katherine’s door throwing up blood, we see the aftermath of her being treated in the hospital, along with Carson and Rapp catching up on everything that’s occurred up to this point.

As Billy meets with Carson and Rapp at the hospital, we’re given a handful of details as to what happened with Lily, including that she experienced some type of trauma, they found both hallucinogens and chicken blood in her body, she threw up a tooth, and that she was 8 weeks pregnant – but not anymore.

With Lily being only 14 years old, this is alarming and horrific for multiple reasons. As Geena eventually allows Carson into Lily’s hospital room, the truth is finally revealed: Henry raped Lily. As she explains the details of that night, we see a flashback of Henry in a floral crown holding a chicken at one of his parties that he invited Lily to, where she also believed she was drugged as she couldn’t tell real from fake during portions of the night.

During the act, she remembered seeing Logan standing in the corner, listening. Afterwards and before she passed out in the bed, Henry said she was just drunk and she was misremembering what had happened. She starts to question if it was actually her fault, and instantly Carson and Geena tell her it was absolutely not.

After Lily shared her frightening experience, Geena went to report it to the police – however, Eckert wouldn’t submit the report. He ended up going to her home and trying to bribe her with $50,000 to keep quiet about it all.

Even after bringing Lily to the hospital the next day to get a sexual assault forensic exam, Geena all of a sudden saw Eckert show up, who forced them to leave and go back to their house. He went as far as physically assaulting her and breaking her wrist, threatening that if they tell anyone about the sexual assault, the next person will be hurt even worse. “He’s on the [Parks’] payroll,” Geena told Carson, “I thought you were too. Sometimes I think the whole fucking town is on the payroll.”

Right as we think the details of Lily’s trauma are finished, she informs both Carson and her mom for the first time how she found out she was pregnant (one week prior) and the steps she went through to terminate the pregnancy the night before. Due to being afraid of getting an abortion at the hospital because of the Parks’ power in the town, Lily went with a suggestion from Pam – to go to Laney and complete a ritual at a cabin in the woods.

We see flashbacks of people in the witch masks in the same clearing of the woods that Rapp previously found, with chickens and bones around as Lily describes what she had to do. This included swallowing Henry’s tooth, which had fallen out of his mouth after Pam had previously punched him, and killing and drinking the blood of a chicken as people chanted around her. After being left alone eventually, she felt very sick and walked back to town – making it only as far as Katherine’s house. When asked by Carson why Lily hadn’t told her mom about the pregnancy, Lily deflected, saying she was tired.

“Ya know, I wish I had killed both of them"

It’s apparent that Carson thinks Geena killed Logan and did something to Henry, as she recounts her own sexual assault from high school, and says how her mom wanted to kill the guy who did it to her. She tries to create a safe space for Geena to admit it, as she finally says, “Ya know, I wish I had killed both of them,” and continues stating she was happy when she heard Logan was dead – and she hopes wherever Henry is, that he’s dead, too.

At this point, we see Rapp has found out Geena returned a rental car the same day he checked his out and saw the box with the podcast recording in it – he assumes she left it in his car for him to find, so he breaks into her house to see if he can find anything suspicious. As he’s later on the phone with Carson, who’s filling him in on the revelations and reminding him they have to listen to more of Logan’s tapes to hear the sexual assault, Rapp hears Geena come home. The sound of her opening the door startles him and he knocks a carton of eggs from the counter onto the ground – they immediately break and spread all over the floor.

As Geena walks into the kitchen and sees the broken eggs, she instantly goes to her closet to grab a shotgun, right as Rapp is running out of the house as quickly as he can. He bolts into the backyard and hides behind her chicken coop, where she sees him go and fires a warning shot at the coop. She slowly walks around to find him holding up a shovel in defense, and then we see the sudden shock on her face as she lowers her gun and is staring at something on the ground behind Rapp.

Rapp, confused, turns around to see what she’s looking at – and we see Henry’s corpse lying in the chicken coop. The camera slowly pans up his naked, bruised body, and we see – just like Logan – Henry has also been castrated.

Somber music follows as we see Eckert take Geena away in handcuffs, along with Henry’s body being transported to the morgue.

The episode winds down with Carson inviting Rapp to her place – which is a cozy houseboat – and he shares more about his past and present working for the Parks, including how his dad did the dirty work for the family, cleaning horrible situations like this up for them.

As he’s processing his grief and feelings, Rapp admits he thinks he knew Henry was this type of person – despite always seeing him as a little brother and not wanting to believe it – due to allegations and situations that occurred in the past where the Parks paid people off to make things disappear. “But never with a minor,” he says, still looking shocked.

Carson alludes to Eckert making a move on her the night before (when Rapp was with Katherine and ignoring her texts) as she herself is processing how he could do something as awful as to try and cover up Lily’s sexual assault. During their conversation, Rapp also makes clear that he knows Geena didn’t kill Henry. He said the shocked look on her face was a major tell that she had no idea he was lying there dead in her backyard. The last two episodes will hopefully reveal the truth regarding whether Geena did kill him or who is framing her.

The vibe starts changing as the two of them begin to sit closer together and start flirting sweetly with one another, with Rapp saying how he “wants to kick the shit out of Eckert” the next time he sees him, even though he knows Carson handled things on her own.

They start kissing and getting intimate – even though Rapp flirts with everyone and just slept with Katherine literally the night before, there’s an underlying sweetness to the two of them together in this scene. An honesty that seems to come across when he’s with Carson specifically, and he tells her, “You’re so fucking beautiful” right before they have sex. It feels like he genuinely might mean it.

The narrator closes out the episode while we see more shots of Carson and Rapp together, as she says, “A witch with a child would never die, and wouldn’t that be fucking scary?”

Episode 6 has a theme of witches without children, with multiple narrations referencing it throughout, and the various references to pregnancy make you wonder if Carson will potentially end up getting pregnant after what happens in this scene… or if they’re going in an entirely different direction for the last two episodes.

As we wrap up this latest episode, perfectly titled, “Mother Witch,” it seems more obvious that Baba Yaga and the “witches” in the masks are more likely strong women from the town who are trying to protect one another from the horrors around them – by any means necessary. This would explain the suspicions of Katherine, Olena, and even Pam, as they tend to hold back knowledge while also forming relationships with Henry and Logan.

The final two episodes of Yaga will be airing together on November 27.

items.title: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall is in select theaters on November 20.

Paul Thomas Anderson’s concert movie, Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall,is as stripped-back and threadbare as they come in keeping with its subject: a minimalist solo concert by Geese front man Cameron Winter. The twenty-four-year-old folk artist — twenty-three at the time of filming — sits at a piano on a darkened stage, titled away from the audience, creating a gentle mystery of sorts which Anderson complements with his camera, operated on occasion by producer Benny Safdie. The result will no doubt depend on your interest in Winter’s music, but the documentary evokes a grounded tactility that’s hard to ignore, and whose allure is harder to deny.

With the beeps and boops of mobile ticket scanners, Anderson welcomes us inside the titular concert hall (How do you get there?!) before a hard cut from empty stands to a full and bustling crowd creates anticipation. It’s a far cry from the filmmaker’s other concert movie — the Jodhpur-set Junun — which made use of digital tech like drones to gawk at its Indian musicians like animals in a zoo. Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall feels far more compassionate, as though its director either felt closer to the music or had simply reached greater maturity as a documentarian.

The dim concert space comes alive thanks to the grain of Anderson’s 35mm film — across several cameras — creating an image that feels fluid and rhythmic, even in static moments. It feels no less enveloping even when on-screen audience members occasionally display a lack of etiquette with their cellphones (the movie is, in this way, quite complete and immersive… for better or worse). Between wide shots of Winter hunched over his piano and close-ups of him circling the microphone, surrounded practically by a void, the frame conjures imagery reminiscent of one of the artist’s prominent tracks, “,” in which he croons: “You were meant to watch my private ceremonies, all in the dark parts of rooms.”

There’s both a religiosity and self-effacing quality to Winter’s poetry, which speaks for itself through the music without Anderson really employing any flourishes beyond the show’s own direction. Lights intermittently come up to illuminate a sparse backdrop reminiscent of an empty home mid-transition, which we’re allowed to glimpse at times. Most of the time, however, the frame is occupied by close-ups of Winter lost in soulful song.

Even those unfamiliar with Winter’s music will be taken by his dreamlike reflections, peppered with humor through piano peacocking on the highest keys and a funny interaction with the set itself. 

It’s the kind of soothing concert film you could probably zone out or fall asleep to, which is by no means a bad thing in this particular context. Even those unfamiliar with Winter’s music will likely be taken by his dreamlike reflections, peppered with occasional humor through some piano peacocking on the highest keys and a particularly funny interaction with the set itself. But for the most part, the doc and its central performance are as straightforward and classical as they come, even though the music has a modern, alternative vibe.

With slow zooms and push-ins — and on the rarest of occasions, a hand-held follow — Anderson’s approach verges on reverential for the young musical prodigy, which is in keeping with the demands of his late-2025 live show. It’s about the resplendent music more than anything else, including the performance itself, which exists more in the echoes off Carnegie Hall’s historic walls than even the stage from which it emanates, decorated only with intermittent wires. Much like the concert’s designers have chosen to do, Anderson essentially gets out of the way despite having a camera practically affixed to Winter himself — one he keeps entirely invisible until the closing credits, revealing his own illusions only once Winter’s magic has ceased after a mellifluous 72 minutes.

items.title: Percy Jackson and the Olympians Season 3, Episodes 1 & 2 Recap and Review
items.author: Jacob Kienlen
items.content:
The premiere of Percy Jackson Season 3 marks the first time an adaptation has made it past the second novel in Rick Riordan's series. For those who haven't read The Titan's Curse, you'll notice there's a shift in tone right off the bat. The characters are older, the stakes feel higher, and everything has gotten a bit more serious. The start of Season 3 brings that much-needed weight to the story, largely thanks to how well the cast has grown into their roles.

The first two episodes act as the setup for the main quest of Season 3. We get a proper introduction to Thalia as a key player, as well as new characters like Nico, Bianca, Artemis, Apollo, and Atlas. The premiere largely succeeds in its effort to kick off the story, and by the end of Episode 2 I found myself genuinely excited for more.

Walker Scobell has been a delightful Percy Jackson since Season 1, but he's only gotten better with experience. Whenever Percy is interacting with his friends or the gods themselves, all of the moving parts of the story seem to click in place. Tamara Smart also makes for a great Thalia, acting as the perfect counterbalance to Percy. These are two equally powerful demigods who are learning to deal with each other's existence, and the tension definitely comes through. The most engaging moments of the first two episodes are when the son of Poseidon and the daughter of Zeus find themselves at odds—which is pretty much constantly.

These characters are really starting to feel less like kids and more like dangerous half-bloods you don't want to mess with.

Godlike powers are also on full display in Season 3. Percy has had time to grow into his abilities and we get a taste of that in the very first scene. Now that Thalia is no longer stuck as a tree, we also get to see a spark of Zeus' wrath in action. Director James Bobin does an excellent job of incorporating these magical elements in a way that doesn't feel overdone. Getting to see Percy subtly block an arrow with a splash of water or Thalia paralyze a few enemies with a bit of lightning is quite fun to watch and also builds perfectly toward the massive clash of power that Percy and Thalia's rocky start was leading us to the whole time. These characters are really starting to feel less like kids and more like dangerous half-bloods you don't want to mess with.

While the core performances are excellent throughout, the series stumbles a bit in these first two episodes when the gods take center stage. Dafne Keen does a decent job of embodying Artemis' intensity, but she feels a bit out of pace with the rest of the cast when she's actually interacting with them. This feeling is further intensified by her very uncomfortable interactions with her brother Apollo (Hubert Smielecki) that just aren't believable at all. Thankfully these moments are a pretty minor occurrence and don't weigh down the rest of the story for long. Jason Mantzoukas' Dionysus is, of course, the exception to this and I loved every moment he had on screen so far.

items.title: Yellowjackets Season 4, Episode 1 Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
Season 4, Episode 1 – “Hivemind,” which is streaming now on Paramount+. New episodes drop weekly on Fridays.

In 2012, Showtime delivered , its best original horror drama since . Featuring a female-led cast of middle-aged legends (Melanie Lynskey, Tawny Cypress, Christina Ricci, etc.) and mostly unknowns playing their younger selves, Yellowjackets earned instant buzz for its scary mix of survival horror, social hierarchy commentary and trauma manifestations. So it’s been hugely disappointing that the subsequent two seasons have only offered diminishing returns as creators Ashley Lyle and Bart Nickerson (Narcos) haven’t been able to extend the potency of their original premise into coherent and compelling past and present narratives walking into Season 4.

As this is the final season, there was plenty of hope that the writing team would pour all of their reserved ideas into purposeful and emotionally rewarding narratives ignited by the plane crash survivors getting rescued from their feral, cannibalistic ways in the Canadian wilderness. Let’s be real: their return to society has long been past due as they’ve killed or eaten two-thirds of the cast. The fourth season premiere episode, “Hivemind,” crackles with the excitement of that anticipated reentry, told through 1998-era TV breaking news announcements, including Gen Z stalwart MTV News. But then Yellowjackets falls back into its bad habits, like leaning on needle drop montages to Nirvana’s “Where Did You Sleep Last Night” to show the broken and battered survivors being examined in the hospital, instead of giving them meaty scenes where they can process the moment with consequential words and deeds.

The present day storyline picks up in the aftermath of Melissa’s (Hilary Swank) murder of Van (Lauren Ambrose). The formerly hidden in plain sight survivor grabs her wife Alex (Jaylee Hamidi) and young daughter to flee the retribution of Tai (Cypress), Shauna (Lynskey) and Misty (Ricci). However, that’s fear wasted because the trio are a rather listless group now. Tai and Misty don’t trust Shauna anymore so they’re quietly plotting, black comedy style, to make their unstable frenemy believably “disappear.”

Season 4 has 10 episodes to land wherever this is going, and so far, the episodes aren’t making a case that this couldn’t have just all wrapped up a season earlier.

Shauna has ostracized everyone in her life, including her estranged husband Jeff (Warren Kole) and fellow murderous daughter Callie (Sarah Desjardins). With nothing else to do, she continues to scream at the world, as evidenced by several slightly humorous scenes where Lynskey gives it her all in displaying Shauna’s hair-trigger and unapologetic rage. Unfortunately, surface anger is all the writers are giving Lynskey to play in these early episodes, so there’s no nuance or pathos to make any of it feel scary or even sympathetic. Though it’s clear the writers think Shauna is a punk rock paragon of female retribution, they’re only giving her cartoonish scenarios to express herself, which doesn’t temper the fact that she’s a multi-murderer with issues that keep getting kicked down the narrative road – likely to the last episodes of this season.

While two parallel plots have always been plenty for the series — and out of balance interest- wise since the middle of Season 2 — the writers have introduced another side plot to just before the soccer team survivors are rescued. These surprise asides fill in the unknown details between the hunt for Mari (Alexa Barajas) and Nat’s (Sophie Thatcher) success in using the satellite phone in the Season 3 finale. But to be frank, who cares? The past is the past and these extra tidbits don’t move the needle in absolving these kids of the multitude of sins they’ve already agreed to keep to themselves. The show is giving precious story real estate to the minutiae instead of leaning into scenes happening after their New Jersey return, and it’s baffling filler.

Yellowjackets Season 4 has 10 episodes to land wherever this is going, and so far, the episodes aren’t making a case that this couldn’t have just all wrapped up a season earlier. The groundwork is obviously being set for an escalation between an unrepentant Melissa and rage-monster Shauna, with Tai and Misty as cagey observers. Hopefully, that builds into something plausible and worthwhile, because the 1998 reentry story for the survivors is already meandering and so slow that nothing of note is revealed that we don’t already know from prior seasons. It’s filling in gaps and that’s not great television.

items.title: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth Review
items.author: Jim Vejvoda
items.content:
David Fincher may be the director of The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, but this follow-up to Once Upon a Time in Hollywood is a Quentin Tarantino film through and through. Tarantino’s screenplay, with its novelistic structure and signature oh-so-cool dialogue, is what gives The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth its distinctive rhythm and vibe. Fincher’s exquisite filmmaking eye is still evident throughout, but Cliff Booth is the director’s least emotionally grueling film to date, bereft of the obsessiveness and psychological darkness that’s long been a hallmark of his work. And while Cliff Booth may be David Fincher’s most fun (and funniest) movie, its leisurely pacing and abrupt conclusion may still leave viewers divided.

Taking place over the course of several days in June 1977, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth finds Brad Pitt’s former stuntman now scraping by as a bartender and also a projectionist at the New Beverly Cinema, an iconic LA theater that Tarantino has owned for the past couple of decades . But instead of playing that summer’s biggest new release, Star Wars, the New Bev is showing blaxploitation films starring former football player-turned-action star Roderick “Hot Rod” Harrison, played with smooth command by Yahya Abdul-Mateen II. (Hot Rod is basically Fred “The Hammer” Williamson, right down to being a former Oakland Raider.)

Cliff also tends bar at a mud wrestling venue, where he makes margaritas for droves of adoring women. And when he’s not working, he’s looking after his elderly dad Gus, played with lovable gruffness by RoboCop’s Peter Weller. But as we know from Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, Cliff is a tough man with a mysterious and violent past.

Cliff may no longer work in Hollywood – Rick Dalton (played by Leonardo DiCaprio in that earlier film) got too fat for him to double and eventually went off to Australia to star in a TV series called Dingo Dan – but Hollywood still needs Cliff’s services as a fixer every now and then. When Cliff is approached by talent agent Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), they both think it’s to help her TV superstar client Charlie Peters (Scott Caan) prepare for his upcoming role.

But Charlie soon reveals to Cliff the real reason he needs help from the Tinseltown legend known for beating up Bruce Lee and killing those hippies who broke into Rick Dalton’s house. Charlie is in deep trouble with the Verdusco brothers (played by Matt Groove and JB Tadena), a pair of Filipino gangsters intent on killing him if he doesn’t repay the debt he owes them. There’s more to Charlie’s dilemma than that, but that’s the gist of it.

Tarantino’s story, which he’s likened to an Elmore Leonard novel, unfolds at an ambling pace, soaking in the quieter moments with its colorful cast of characters and enjoying the minutiae of their daily lives for much of the film’s roughly two-hour-and-20-minute runtime. The movie will surely try some viewers’ patience as it rambles along until its violent and abrupt ending, a conclusion certain to leave some people with nagging questions.

The plot involving the Verdusco brothers, Charlie and Cliff doesn’t really start paying off until later in the film, but when it does, things get very bloody and very brutal very fast. That said, I still found the violence to be a bit more restrained than in the films Tarantino has directed himself. It’s the smaller, human moments between the characters in this film that have stayed with me, though, such as Cliff’s humorous courtship of Karen and his gentle relationship with his dad. And, as in Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, there’s a lot of nerdy joy to be found in Tarantino’s alternate history, which is rife with faux films and TV shows that seem like they could have – should have – existed at that time. As with Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is a story told by an older, more thoughtful artist aware that time is short and things are changing. Cliff Booth may be Tarantino’s avatar for being the last cool guy in Hollywood with zero fucks left to give.

The film boasts great performances across the board, beginning with Pitt’s rugged reprisal of his Oscar-winning role. Cliff still has that same effortless cool as before, but he’s more of a human pincushion now, his comfortability with pain and violence making him the perfect guy to deal with the kind of dirty jobs no one else wants to handle. And as the lead this time around, Cliff isn’t nearly as laconic as he was in the previous film.
