If the first film was all about capturing Cliff’s mystique, then the sequel wants you to get to know him.

Elizabeth Debicki makes Karen Crosby real and not a cliche Hollywood suit. She’s smart and led a life before this career, which requires her to be everything from a deal-maker to a babysitter for needy clients like Charlie. As Charlie, Scott Caan gives a career-best performance as a short, Robert Conrad-like actor who does his own stunts in an array of Quinn Martin-style TV series. He’s also married to faded actress Toni, played with a mix of grit and “still got it” sexy charm by Carla Gugino. And as the Verdusco brothers, Matt Groove and JB Tadena command your attention whenever they’re on screen, with both actors finding the quirks and humor in their otherwise fearsome characters.

items.title: Madden Review
items.author: Jim Vejvoda
items.content:
is now streaming on Prime Video.

David O. Russell’s erratically directed Madden is an assemblage of montages in search of a story. Is Madden about the relationship between Oakland Raiders coach John Madden and team owner Al Davis? Is it about John’s struggles to be a husband and father when football’s no longer consuming his life? Is it about John proving himself as an announcer? Is it about the creation of EA’s Madden video game franchise?

Madden the movie casts a wide net around all those topics while never satisfactorily exploring them in any real depth or detail, the whole endeavor playing out like SNL skit after SNL skit without anything ever feeling emotionally genuine. It’s one frantically edited, half-explored sequence set to vintage needledrops after another.

is packed into a fat suit and prosthetics as the NFL icon, coming across more like a stage actor starring in Shrek the Musical than a real flesh-and-blood person. Yes, John Madden was an over-the-top figure in real life but the movie and Cage turn him into a cartoon character or the big, bumbling oafish dad in a sitcom. ( was reportedly up to play Madden before Cage.)

Christian Bale is similarly reduced to makeup and mugging as Al Davis, only occasionally hinting at a real person underneath that greasy, gaudy exterior. Davis’ drive to “just win, baby” certainly fed Madden’s hunger for the game and for victory on the field. Their symbiotic relationship here tries to be the film’s main focus, but the slight story never digs much deeper than the superficial.

John and Al seem made for each other but there's almost a manipulative pusher and junkie dynamic at play. At one point, John tries to break free from Al’s hold over him, but the film is reluctant to show any of its characters in too negative a light.

For both Madden and Davis, it’s their wives – Virginia Madden and Carol Davis, respectively – who help illuminate their larger-than-life spouse’s vulnerabilities, with Kathryn Hahn faring better than Sienna Miller in having an impact. As Virginia, Hahn finds the humor and heart in an otherwise underwritten character (Miller’s Carol is the far more thankless role). Still, Hahn’s is arguably the most emotionally genuine performance in the film.

After a few teases early on, the last half hour of the movie hones in on the creation of . This sequence finally offers the movie a bit more focus and some conflict between John and Al, as the latter doesn’t want John to contribute his time and knowledge to what he deems an inconsequential endeavor when he could come back to work for the Raiders. The SNL skit vibe of the whole film isn’t helped by the casting of John Mulaney as EA’s Trip Hawkins, with the entire EA staff and their endeavor depicted as a bunch of nerds who learn how to be jocks thanks to John Madden’s football know-how.

It’s all pretty condescending. The EA staff are all portrayed as stereotypical geeks, right down to their costuming. In reality, EA’s video game designers of that time were depicted as being akin to rock musicians, not hapless dweebs. Still, there might have at least been a fun Revenge of the Nerds-style film in here had Madden chosen to just chronicle this one chapter of John Madden’s life. Instead, the film is merely a highlight reel, with none of Madden’s accomplishments feeling any more special than the rest.

Between 2022’s Amsterdam and now Madden, director David O. Russell has lost his filmmaking footing after a decade-plus of solid movies (Three Kings, , , ). Madden is bewildering in its sloppiness and inability to commit to telling a focused story that does its beloved subject justice.

items.title: Dig Review
items.author: Michael Peyton
items.content:
Minor spoilers below for Dig, streaming November 23 on Peacock.

Dig is a gem of a TV show, even if it takes a while to pull it from the ground. The new workplace comedy from Amy Poehler and Mike Schur, who previously worked together on the long-running sitcom Parks and Recreation, takes standard issue office hijinx, moves them to a sun-drenched European locale, and weaves in a propulsive mystery that Agatha Christie would be proud of.

Poehler stars as Elise, the prickly but loveable site manager of an archaeological dig site in Greece. Elise spends her days searching for buried antiquities, wrangling a cadre of horny, fumbling students, and keeping tabs on her pompous dinosaur of a boss, played by Hugh Laurie with a sense of comedic melancholy.

When Elise is passed over for a promotion after dig leader Neville (Laurie) decides to stick around for another year, she promptly stumbles upon a one-of-a-kind buried artifact and draws a group of colleagues into a web of secrets and mysteries. It’s a shame it takes a while for the show to get rolling because, once it does, it’s thrilling and hilarious.

All 10 episodes of Dig premiere at once on Peacock. The binge drop is nothing new but, for this show in particular, is a lifesaver. The first few episodes are funny enough, but often drag to the point of being boring. The action starts in medias res, with Elise and three of her colleagues — ditzy Patty (Fina Strazza), prim Clare (Antonia Thomas), and vivacious Dylan (Geraldine Viswanathan) — caught in a slapstick brawl involving biting, punching, someone getting shot in the leg, and a character falling into a giant pit. (What’s up with Mike Schur, Amy Poehler, and people falling into fictional pits?) But when we flash back several weeks to the main timeline of the show, things slow down substantially.

We spend several episodes introducing a wide cast of characters, the myriad ins and outs of archaeology and dig sites, and the various dramatic backstories and relationships of each of our main characters. We find out Dylan left Elise hanging years prior when the two wanted to start their own dig together while Clare is engaged to her perfectly fine colleague Randy (Jon Pointing) but longs for something more. Patty is a naive farm girl seeing the world for the first time. All of this setup is necessary for any show to be truly durable, but the first several episodes of Dig risk forsaking an engaging plot by spending too much time meandering through the characters’ histories.

Halfway through the season, Dig hits the accelerator and doesn’t look back until the finale’s credits cut to black. The buried artifact Elise found — and promptly shared with only a select group of colleagues — is stolen and the show kicks into high gear with double crosses, character development, and farce. The show’s central mystery — Who stole the artifact and where is it? — allows the writers to throw their characters in numerous, high-pressure situations (Infiltrating a fancy party! A walk of shame in front of a hook-up’s scolding mother! A road full of sheep!) that both propel the plot forward and dig deeper into what makes those characters tick.

As Elise, Poehler plays against type as a weary, often grumpy midlevel site manager. She still serves plenty of one-liners and uses her immense acting chops and top-tier timing to weave together the show’s comedic and dramatic elements. It’s miles away from the sunny, hyper-driven Leslie Knope, but it’s still a marvelous performance. It can be jarring to see Poehler, known for her laugh-out-loud performances across movies and TV, play what amounts to the straight man here, but she translates Elise’s frustrations, longing for the top job, and drive into a fully drawn character.

Poehler’s zag allows for three of her main co-stars to alternate driving the show’s more laugh-out-loud moments. As Dylan, Viswanathan takes the role that Poehler would have played 20 years ago: a bawdy party girl who came back to the dig to get back at her ex-boyfriend and wears ballcaps with crude language while dining out. Thomas’s Clare is a counterweight: proper, intelligent, and striving to prove to her rich, controlling mother that she can be her own woman. Which brings us to Patty.

As the naive, cornfed graduate assistant who’s brand new to the dig site, Fina Strazza’s breakout character is both endearing and lights-out hilarious. From delivering ditzy one-liners to playing a scene against a talking scorpion to runs of incredible physical comedy (there’s a bit with a water bottle and a tube of sunscreen that I can’t get out of my head), Strazza propels what could be a one-dimensional character into a scene-stealing performance.

Once they establish their relationship dynamics, Poehler, Viswanathan, Thomas, and Strazza are unstoppable together. They create a solid core of characters with shifting loyalties that the writers constantly pick apart and reshuffle to great effect.

The cast is rounded out by a who’s who of Schur-verse standbys. Jason Mantzoukas shows up as a dig site looter. Mo Collins is hilarious as someone Patty meets in a hot tub. Rashida Jones even cameos. It’s a palette Schur has played with before to great effect in shows like Parks and Recreation, The Good Place, and a stint on the American version of The Office. But what Dig has that those shows don’t is a sense of adventure and genre inventiveness.

The sun-drenched Grecian locale (which, let’s face it, is obviously a CGI’d Southern California for the most part) is almost irrelevant, which is odd to consider given the show’s reliance on archaeology and history as its central theme. While the distinct outdoor nature of the show does make it stand out against more standard sitcom fare, the skill with which the cast and creators of Dig eventually blend both comedy and thrills would make it a must-watch show if it was set in a strip mall parking lot.

It’s also nice to have a show like Dig be unafraid of actually moving the story along. Once the plot gets going, storylines are deftly planted, executed, and resolved. There are no drawn-out will-they-won’t-they relationships. Characters are free to be multidimensional with motivations rooted in moral gray areas. Poehler herself drops more f-bombs throughout the season than you’d ever have expected.

It all amounts to a show that’s both familiar and inventive. The pop culture references, puns, and sarcastic asides that are foundational to every Mike Schur sitcom are still there. A motley cast of characters gets themselves into more jams than you can possibly count. Characters pair off in scene after scene, creating in-universe in-jokes that circle back episodes later. But Dig also takes the classic half-hour TV comedy and breathes some life into the format by inserting some great thrills and mystery. While it takes way too long to kick into gear, I’m hopeful that the back half of Dig’s first batch of episodes portends a full-throttle Season 2.

items.title: The Altruists Review
items.author: Leanne Butkovic
items.content:
This is a spoiler-free review of (though can you really spoil real life?). The eight-episode series is now streaming on Netflix.

2022 was a banner year for TV shows based on true stories about tech CEOs behaving badly, fraudsters, and sometimes both: The Dropout, WeCrashed, Inventing Anna, Super Pumped. It was also the same year that the crypto exchange FTX and the crypto hedge fund Alameda Research filed for bankruptcy, revealing that the two companies founded by Sam Bankman-Fried, “the J.P. Morgan of crypto,” and his math whiz business partner/on-off girlfriend Caroline Ellison were not just closely affiliated; Alameda was funding trades with FTX customers’ money to the tune of $8 billion.

2026 is another standout year for similar entertainment: You Can See Everything, The Social Reckoning, Musk, Artificial. Once again, FTX is in the mix, this time via The Altruists, an eight-episode Netflix series that traces the rise and fall of “” and Ellison, dubbed the Bonnie and Clyde of crypto. While it’s at times maybe more sentimental than it needed to be in humanizing the two, The Altruists doesn’t hold back on its assessment of Bankman-Fried and Ellison as two unpleasant weirdos who knew how to draw the worst out of each other.

Created by Graham Moore, who won the adapted screenplay Oscar in 2015 for The Imitation Game, and based on reporting by New York Magazine, The Altruists begins with the end. Audio news clips about FTX and Alameda’s bankruptcy scandal play over to Anthony Boyle’s Bankman-Fried seconds from being arrested, screening a call from Ellison (an unrecognizable Julia Garner). Before he decides whether to answer, it cuts back to 2016 as Bankman-Fried practices human reactions in the mirror during his early days as a money-making savant at the quant trading firm Jane Street, where he met Ellison.

The Altruists jumps across timelines throughout, and it’s largely effective. In bopping between the contrasting rosy early days and the tension-wracked lead-up to the FTX collapse, the parallel edits serve as a useful tool in watching just how much of their souls Bankman-Fried and Ellison sold to keep their companies afloat. They were up to some risky, sketchy stuff from the beginning, but it was in the pursuit of following the ethos of effective altruism, a philosophical movement popular in tech spaces that, as The Altruists describes it, boils down to the idea of making as much money as possible to give away to charitable causes. But as the director for the Center of Effective Altruism told New York Magazine in 2022: “There has not been a bad actor in history who hasn’t been able to couch their conduct behind some meaningful and generally positive ideology.” (The front of that issue featured a portrait of Bankman-Fried along with the coverline “The Virtue Was the Con.”)

Like its approach to explaining EA, The Altruists maintains a fairly narrow scope ostensibly out of necessity; how easy it would be to go down the rabbit hole of explaining every connection, decision, and detail. It mostly ignores the outside media curiosity to focus on the relationship between Bankman-Fried and Ellison. What the series loses as a result is the bigger picture of just how massive FTX was at its height — though it’s always floating in the background, telegraphed through the sheer amount of wealth shown off on yachts and swanky houses in the Bahamas.

Bankman-Fried was hailed as a visionary, the “next Warren Buffet” who would democratize money, as he cruised through meetings while playing League of Legends. He was invited to the and built relationships with politicians and celebrities. The Altruists, on the other hand, depicts him less flatteringly: He was a socially awkward dork whose best ideas seem to have come from other people. The show isn’t terribly kind to Ellison either: She was a straight-shooter who was into writing smutty Harry Potter fan fiction, LARPing, and polyamory. Boyle and Garner are both excellent as Bankman-Fried and Ellison, each doing an affected character voice that is perfectly grating. But Garner — who played a different scammer, Anna Delvey, in Netflix’s Inventing Anna — is the highlight, sinking into her role to the point the prosthetics started to seem like natural extensions of her face.

The script’s one major flaw is something that doesn’t really have an alternative, more elegant workaround. Despite the attempt to simplify a complicated story, The Altruists still needs to explain finance and economic concepts to a Netflix audience. It spells these things out by putting two of its (very smart!) characters into conversations where one brings up a concept, i.e. a prisoner’s dilemma, the other person rebukes them saying they “know what it is,” and then the first person continues to explain it anyway. Again, it’s a hard problem to get around if jargon-spouting, a la Industry, isn’t the goal. Even if it’s laid out in broader strokes, The Altruists wants the audience to grasp just who these people are and what they’ve done.

items.title: Grand Theft Auto 6 Review
items.author: Alex Garcia
items.content:
During my first dozen-or-so hours with Grand Theft Auto 6, I fixed my leaky roof, collected some rum from a shady liquor store, played way too many games of pool, read a book about World War 2 soldiers with a penchant for teabagging, and caught a lot of fish. On the more ridiculous end of the spectrum, I also temporarily… a luxury yacht called Party on the Poop Deck before running it aground and drinking its owner’s beer, slapped the crap out of a bloke who cursed at me, found a finger in my horniest neighbour’s plumbing, threatened an alligator wearing a hat, and got mugged by a drunk sea captain with a harpoon gun – before stealing his weapon while he peed in a garden.

Over 100 hours later, I’ve now completely lost track of all the things I’ve seen and done within GTA 6’s astounding open world – and I see no real limit to the amount of time I could spend here, endlessly exploring and interacting with Vice City and the massive area surrounding it. While the well-paced story effectively nudged me around the map, there are still vast sections of it that I’m yet to even visit – despite hitting the credits after almost 120 hours of hijinks. Frankly, I’ve never played anything that’s hit quite like GTA 6 – and right now I have zero plans to playing it.

Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos are an interesting pair of playable characters, and unlike any leads that have come before them in the series. Their motivations and goals are very different from the main characters of previous GTA games, and their priority is really about escape rather than revenge or empire building. They’re not angels, and it invariably their recklessness as small-time crooks that puts them in the wrong place at the wrong time, but the overall sliminess of their far more powerful antagonists does make the couple easy to root for throughout their story – which unfolds like four or five seasons of a prestige TV show.

My Jason and Lucia maintained a professional criminal rating throughout thanks to my style of play, where I opt for clean escapes, stealth, and non-lethal takedowns against general law enforcement if feasible, disabling vehicles by popping tyres rather than pummelling the windscreens with gunfire, and leaving civilians unharmed as often as possible. By the end of the story, I had actually only killed 11 civilians, all of which would’ve been unfortunate accidents.

Jason, a capable yet calm and softly spoken army veteran, is a natural fit for GTA. He remains mostly a mystery throughout, but his quiet cowboy demeanour doesn’t stray too far from Red Dead Redemption 2’s Arthur Morgan, and I like that. Lucia, who’s headstrong but not abrasive and confident but not cocky, gets to showcase a wider range of emotions. She’s easily the most likeable and multifaceted woman in the history of the series, and it’s abundantly clear that GTA’s writing has grown up dramatically in the last 13 years – and that RDR2 has had nothing but positive effects on its sister series.

This is a world that feels more lived-in and real than anything I’ve ever played.

We play mostly as Jason for the opening phase of Chapter 1, but it’s a smart way of easing us into the many systems we need to come to grips with (there’s a full help menu to explain any controls or actions you might forget). In the time it takes to start and many typical shooters and action games, I’d lived several days of a second life as Jason, who spends a good deal of his time on the wrong side of the law couriering drug shipments up and down the Leonida Keys but otherwise keeps a low profile in the relatively quiet tourist town he calls home. There’d been strife and there’d been shootouts, sure, but the main thread of the story had barely begun: Lucia was yet to re-enter the picture, I’d not even visited Vice City itself at all, and I was entirely content to while away hours messing around with GTA 6’s many, many distractions.

It’s ironic, perhaps, that some of its distractions are actually games themselves – Jason has a PlayStation-style console in his home featuring three playable games, and his local bar has a darkly humorous riff on classic Buck Hunter cabinets I kept getting sucked into. Straight away, it’s evident this is not a world of painted-on backdrops and empty props. This is a world that feels more lived-in and real than anything I’ve ever played, and it’s one you can interact with at a level never seen before in the series. Yes, it was a long wait, but believe me when I say Rockstar has truly pushed the boat out (which, handily enough, is also something you can do yourself in GTA 6 if you find yourself beached).

I’ll readily admit I’m an easy mark for a game like this. I love action movies, car chases, and dad rock, and GTA 6 holds precisely the same things near and dear. I won’t list the long catalogue of movie references I’ve spotted since it’s way more satisfying to recognise them yourself. I also won’t spoil any of the specific needle drops Rockstar finds itself indulging in more than ever – one of which has become one of my favourite moments in the entire series. It does take over the dial a bit more than usual for key moments, but it’s always to great effect, and it certainly hasn’t come at the cost of any reduced focus on radio stations. The mammoth tracklist otherwise includes the return of classic stations V-Rock, Emotion, and Vice City FM, all of which are absolutely overflowing with solid gold (as is new metal station The Chamber). Just those four stations alone – which account for the lion’s share of my listening – feature nearly between them.

In a considerable blow for any company trying to sell me a next-generation console in the near future, GTA 6 also looks even better than it sounds. Allow me to freely concede I’ve never been fussy about frame rates, so long as they don’t constantly fluctuate. For all the hand-wringing I’ve observed over the fact that GTA 6 is locked to 30 frames-per-second – just as Rockstar’s most recent cowboy masterpiece was, not for nothing – I simply did not care in the slightest while I was actually playing. What matters to me is that it looks absolutely incredible and runs smoothly and reliably on a standard PS5. I find all the brilliant visual flourishes far more important, from the concentric rings of ripples on water due to helicopter rotor downwash, to the almost imperceptible line of sweat that appears on Lucia’s forehead after a brisk jog, or the buckling of the fabric on a shirt as torsos twist, to the temporary dents on a punching bag as you strike it. It’s the way long hair rises, whips, and falls over a character’s shoulders and back, whether that’s Lucia’s ponytail swinging back and forth – or my Jason’s luxurious mullet hanging in the air over a motorcycle jump during its brief moment of zero gravity.

It looks absolutely incredible and runs smoothly and reliably on a standard PS5.

This level of detail is seen in other animations, too – dynamic fights which never appear to play out the same way, and the bespoke solutions for characters to slink along the side of a vehicle if the door can’t fully open. Like, there aren’t just animations for operating longarm weapons one-handed if your other hand is full; there’s a separate animation for opening drink cans with one hand as well.

If a sufficiently stable and properly paced 30fps is the route to GTA 6 looking and functioning the way it does, bug-free, then I have no complaints. The sheer density of traffic and pedestrians is stunning, and the graphics at night are supernaturally good. Rockstar allows the world to be realistically dark, giving the lighting room to really flex. It’s honestly jaw-dropping, whether that’s at street level with car headlights and taillights piercing the dark, down on the beach during a late evening storm, or from high above where every light source in the city seems to be individually visible from a distance. Just imagine Microsoft Flight Simulator, only after you land, you can leave the airport, hit a drive-thru, and grab a burger.

The feeling of authenticity is ever-present, and it extends across every element of what you see on screen. For instance, it’s not just that cars look incredible, or that they have – which is something you don’t get in even the very best racing games. It’s that they’re not cars – they’re all car. Maybe the bumper stickers have a story to tell, or there’s bespoke clutter in the tray or trunk. Maybe they belong to a specific business on the map; I’m still seeing vans driving around town with graphics and logos I haven’t noticed before. Maybe they’ve lived a hard life outside in the harsh Leonida sun, the clear coat has flaked away, and they now carry a patina of road grime and dust. Maybe the interior surfaces and seats are worn, maybe they’ve been poorly maintained and belch black exhaust smoke, or maybe they’ve been carefully customised with dazzling neons and truck nuts.

This attention to detail extends to boats, too. Not only have most of them been christened with unique names, but they too are filled with various personal belongings and custom fit-outs. And yes, they can be launched from trailers, put on trailers, and towed to another boat ramp on the other side of the map if you wish. I adore this, and I suspect those who really want to roleplay in this world will too.

At any rate, GTA 6’s dedication to its in-universe car culture is honestly ludicrous, and I love it. There are tuning shops, car salerooms, and motorsport venues all over the map. The fully modelled engines can be restored and switched out. Exhaust and supercharger mods have noticeable effects on a car’s sound. Hell, there’s even a difference in the texture of a hasty Pay ’n’ Spray rush job, which always results in a visible orange peel effect, and a professional respray at a dedicated customisation shop.

The improvements to car damage are massive as well, with GTA 6 more closely resembling something like a slightly scaled-back Wreckfest rather than GTA 5. Lights and mirrors fall off, panels bend and buckle dramatically, and entire wheels can be ripped off before your car becomes fully disabled. Belt an assailant’s head against a nearby car, and it’ll even crater realistically where they bounced off the metal.

Car handling is also the strongest it’s ever been in the series, and it feels a lot more like a refined version of GTA 4 than GTA 5, which is actually great news. It brings back a very tangible sense of heft, only without the overly exaggerated suspension wallow. You can really slide cars properly here, and throwing them into 90-degree corners and perching them on the throttle is now total Hollywood highlight reel stuff. The only thing that really gave me pause was the motorcycle handling, which is quite upright and stiff compared to previous GTAs – I don’t hate it, but it does feel like it comes from a different game altogether.

Car handling is also the strongest it’s ever been in the series.

The decision to opt for more realistic street widths makes for a way more authentic and engaging driving experience, whether you’re cutting up cars on the freeway or cruising the busy beachside strip. GTA 6 is not afraid to trap you behind traffic or roadworks and force you into quick decisions. Do you take the footpath? Do you push through and risk damage? It’s always asking you to think and act, and creates a dynamic to keep you fully engaged.

After a certain point in the story, you’ll get full control to assign Jason and Lucia personal vehicles that actually speak to you, breaking from the preset personal vehicles Michael, Franklin, and Trevor had in GTA 5. For instance, my Jason’s main ride eventually became a fully-built, Marty McFly-style black truck that I sought out and customised specifically. I really appreciate being able to control this element, and you can eventually have a small fleet of personal vehicles at your disposal.

Your car in GTA 6 is very much like your horse in RDR 2, in that it will keep a variety of things safe for you when you’re not carrying (or wearing) them – like stash bags full of stolen goods, longarms, and a handful of outfits. No, you’re no longer able to pull a bazooka out of your back pocket – which may well be a point of contention amongst longtime players who crave the chaotic energy of having a stocked weapon wheel at their constant disposal – but I honestly haven’t missed it. I actually really like the RDR 2 approach of needing to gear up thoughtfully and manually, and it’s neat to see longarms slung over Jason and Lucia’s shoulders or held in their off hand.

Knowing how influential the more measured and deliberate pace of RDR 2 was set to be on GTA 6, I figured I had an idea of how this would translate into Rockstar’s modern crime universe – but even still I was unprepared for how satisfying the shift in attitude would be. It shepherded me into a more lifelike cadence, where I would wake up and eat breakfast or brew a coffee to buff my health, stamina, and focus (which is GTA 6’s consumable slow-motion power-up that functions similarly to Red Dead’s Dead Eye system). Following that, I may take on a story mission before spending the remainder of the day trying out a new fishing spot, playing pool at the bar, or simply exploring the area looking for cool vehicles, secrets, or interesting strangers.

It all very much like RDR 2 as well. Similar to Arthur, Jason and Lucia feel a little heavier than the GTA 5 trio in a pleasing way that grounds them more in the world and gives them a more convincing sensation of inertia as they otherwise seamlessly transition from one action to another. Opponents go down in ever-changing ways, depending on whether you’ve shot to kill or wound – and what you’ve shot them with. Heavy weapons will remove limbs entirely, so keep that in mind if you’re trying to be merciful. Hell, you can even pick up hats and sunglasses from your vanquished foes.

However, while RDR 2’s intimate, smoke-filled shootouts remain some of the best in the business, GTA 6’s firefights are typically orders of magnitude more spectacular thanks to the vastly increased amount of lead you can sling downrange. Gunning helicopters out of the sky is perhaps the most potent example, as sparks shower from the rotors, the mechanics fail, and they spiral down and either break into bits or disappear into enormous fireballs. Helicopters are actually more fragile than ever, and they’re especially susceptible to damage to their tail rotors, but I do love how much more realistic the crashes have subsequently become.

That said, there is a newfound focus on gently encouraging a slightly more empathetic approach when you deal with Leonida’s colourful locals – although, rest assured, the freedom to lash out like a heinous psychopath still exists. If you want to land a jumbo jet on the beach, you still can; you’ll just have to realistically find your way into the cockpit instead of teleporting in from the nose gear. From what I’ve gleaned, it might make sense to have a separate save file for these sorts of shenanigans if you want the story to culminate in a specific way (yes, there are multiple endings). In slightly disappointing news, it doesn’t appear there’s a way to replay previously completed missions from the mission list, which is an unexpected step back from the philosophy embraced by GTA 4: The Ballad of Gay Tony and GTA 5. There is an exhaustive list of cheats that are unveiled after completing the story, which is excellent to see since fun and hilarious cheats are a core part of GTA’s DNA. At least for now, however, the completed missions database is just a series of static thumbs.

The broad love for GTA 4’s Three Leaf Clover bank heist mission is typically regarded as an important trigger for GTA 5’s heavy focus on major heists, and that philosophy has been wonderfully continued in GTA 6. Several massive heists – each with prep work, moving parts, complementary roles for Jason and Lucia, and dramatic crescendos – are all excellent. They unfold within varied and impeccably detailed locations, they benefit greatly from the vastly improved shooting and driving, and they are rewardingly spaced out across the second half of the story. However, what’s particularly interesting is GTA 6’s own brand of Three Leaf Clover’s classic cops ’n’ robbers fantasy, where tense bank robberies aren’t just isolated to scripted missions you can only execute once per playthrough – they’re now something you can pull off in the open world, at will.

Now, you can’t just successfully roll over banks immediately; you need to graduate up to them later in the story once you have the equipment to deal with dye packs. Hit a target with marked bills (or yank an ATM from a wall with a winch) before you have the necessary gear and your take will be lost in an exploding bloom of pink soot that totally coats Jason and/or Lucia and will persistently smear the inside of any vehicle cabin. It’s actually a brilliant visual effect for something I anticipate we’ll all overtly avoid doing more than once.

Bank heists aren’t just isolated to missions – they’re now something you can pull off at will.

However, once banks do become viable targets, all bets are off. Essentially speaking, it’s Three Leaf Clover . No more walking past locked bank branches that can only be engaged with in one-off story missions; now banks are realistic locations that can be entered and cleaned out. That’s a genuinely powerful shift in the long-established GTA crime fantasy. There’s more to it than checking a box and adding another law you can break; it’s about making this living, breathing world around you make more sense than ever. As much as I adore GTA 5, it is invariably discordant that you can bust into a military base and steal a tank, but you can’t and rob a bank. In GTA 6, that hard-to-swallow imbalance is gone. You can simply do both.

Bank jobs in the open world can unfold in multiple ways. Maybe you successfully sneak in the back, find the safe code, get distracted by an office cat, and get sprung by the staff. Maybe you tail an armoured truck pulling up, meaning the vault will be open – making for a bigger payday, plus access to safe deposit boxes. Maybe you stumble in with zero plan, stick around way too long, and completely botch your getaway. Robbing a bank solo typically works out differently from robbing it with your CPU-controlled partner by your side; for instance, head in alone and security might be a little less inclined to outright surrender.

What I find particularly satisfying, however, is how smart you can indeed play it with a little planning. For instance, I’ve been finding banks within a few blocks of multi-storey parking lots great targets to focus on. I park Jason or Lucia’s personal car a few levels up, steal a random getaway ride, and head to the bank. After taking it down, I head straight back to the parking lot as the cops mount their response. After speeding a few floors up, stashing the cash, and changing outfits (you can store a selection of spare clothes in your cars), I can gently cruise past the cops blocking the exit and make a completely clean exfil.

I’m absolutely loving the new, nuanced Wanted system, where the cops can only act on the information they have. I think it’s actually going to be a little frustrating to go back to the likes of GTA 5, where the police magically make a beeline towards you when your crimes cross a certain threshold – even if there are no witnesses, or any believable way for them to know which car you’re driving or what you look like.

There is no longer a radar showing the location of approaching cops, and I haven’t missed it once. Not knowing where the police could be turns evasion into a whole new and more organic experience, where the focus is on scanning the actual world in front of you for threats rather than spending most of your time looking at the minimap. That is, you’re no longer just trying to choose the right streets to leave a hot zone, like Pac-Man trying to route away from the nearest ghosts. You’re listening to the scanner for hints about what the cops know. You’re eyeballing the traffic in the distance, trying to figure out if any of them are police cruisers. It’s knowing when and where to stay out of view entirely, and when it’s safe for you to hide in plain sight. That’s a far bigger thrill.

items.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3, Episodes 5-6 Recap and Review
items.author: Jim Vejvoda
items.content:
The Rings of Power Season 3 loses some forward momentum this week with two very talky episodes where several characters are literally waiting around for something to happen, whether it’s Sauron trying to pry secrets out of Celeborn or the rival Númenórean factions camped across from each other and poised for battle. The closing moments of Episode 306 definitely pick up the pace, though, promising an eventful finish to this season in next week’s final two episodes.

Gil-galad and Elrond’s mission to Númenór to coax Pharazôn into their war against Sauron sees them weighing their options, including the possibility of asking Miriel to rescind her claim to the throne. Ultimately, though, it’s Pharazôn himself who offers to cease hostilities with Miriel by proposing marriage to her. Ick.

That certainly sucks for Miriel – we saw how things went earlier this season for Pharazôn’s previous wife, Eärien – but, for the story, it seems like the only way to resolve this plodding subplot and finally get all the players on the battlefield against Sauron.

Elrond and Gil-galad haven’t been particularly compelling characters this season, but it was nice to see Elrond revisit his past and what his brother Elros meant to him and to the Númenóreans. Indeed, complicated feelings between loved ones and things that had long been left unsaid is a throughline in these episodes not only with Elrond and Elros but also with Galadriel and Celeborn and Durin and Disa as the latter two married couples wrestle with mistakes from the past.

Poor Marnûkh, meanwhile, learns there is a fate worse than death as Sauron slays his children and then leaves him to be tortured. Torture is also used on Celeborn after he’s captured, with the Elf lord getting the Giles Corey treatment. Ultimately, Celeborn is tricked into revealing to Sauron what the missing ingredients are needed to successfully forge the One Ring. That Galadriel-to-Sauron kiss with Celeborn will surely become a gif in no time.

Gandalf’s mission to help Pallando see the light sure didn’t work out well for him, did it? Pallando violently rebuffs Gandalf and sends him away strapped to the back of an oliphaunt. Although I know Gandalf hasn’t reached his full power and potential yet, it was still a bit disappointing to see the Dark Wizard make such quick work of him. I hope the storyline between them can be resolved this season but I suspect it will probably get dragged out into Season 4.

He’s only been a Ring-servant for like a weekend but Theo is already suffering from buyer’s remorse. Galadriel taking pity on him sure is big of her considering he killed Arondir, which makes me suspect Theo will be given a redemptive death in the season finale.

That wouldn’t shock me since this season seems intent on killing off original characters who were introduced in Season 1, whittling the cast down to just the core Tolkien-created characters as the war against Sauron picks up. By doing so, the show is signaling to audiences, “Don’t worry. We know many of you didn’t like these characters, so we’re just gonna make the show more like the movies now.”

items.title: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
The last 14 years have featured a lot of big screen Reapings as YA novelist Suzanne Collins’ dystopian books have been adapted into six individual films. A franchise based on children murdering one another doesn’t exactly scream “blockbuster hit,” but Collins’ reluctant heroine Katniss Everdeen (as embodied by Jennifer Lawrence) captured the hearts and minds of Millennial readers and moviegoers, and so the franchise goes on.

Under the uninterrupted guidance of producer Nina Jacobson and executive producer/director Francis Lawrence, Collins’ surprise standalone prequel books, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes and Sunrise on the Reaping, have also been adapted into big budget movies. The former revealed Coriolanus Snow’s (Tom Blyth) origin story before he turned into a white-haired, totalitarian child killer (Donald Sutherland), while the latter and latest explains the cascading tragedies that created Panem’s lore around Second Quarter Quell victor Haymitch Abernathy, and ultimately why he mentored Katniss and Peeta (Josh Hutcherson) the way he did after their Reaping 24 years later.

While Woody Harrelson brought the perennially sauced Haymitch to vivid life in the first four Hunger Games films, the details about what prompted the character to retreat into booze and solitude primarily remained a mystery. That alone is a decent reason to add another chapter to the franchise — fleshing out the beloved character and giving him his due — but there’s also an equally strong case against fetishizing (again) the bleak and relentlessly punitive Capitol practice of wiping out 24 to 48 children in spectacular fashion. Thankfully, Jacobson and Lawrence cast the hell out of this chapter by featuring an incredible ensemble of generational actors, and most importantly entrusting the emotional heart of the film to Aussie actor Joseph Zada in his star-making performance as young Haymitch.

And though Sunrise sticks to the franchise’s familiar structure of Reaping, tribute training, arena survival, and outcome, screenwriters Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie wisely refashion the details in bold and unexpected ways, resulting in maximum emotional and political impact for a franchise that needs a fresh perspective so it doesn’t devolve into the bread and circuses Collins so astutely satirizes in her books.

Set 24 years before the events of The Hunger Games, this story begins on the 16th birthday of District 12’s affable teen Haymitch Abernathy (​​Joseph Zada). Unfortunately, his day of celebration coincides with the annual Reaping ceremony where Capitol representatives arrive to enforce and broadcast a mandatory lottery that will doom one boy and one girl to compete in the vindictive Hunger Games. Because this year is a Quarter Quell celebration, four children are Reaped, and Haymitch earns his way onto the “team” after he protects his Covey girlfriend, Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak), from speaking out against the Capitol.

As the pack of tributes/neighbors are shuttled to the Capitol, we get to know prickly Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), nervous oddsmaker Wyatt Callow (Ben Wang), and little Louella McCoy (Molly McCann) as they sweat what lays ahead of them. With his Harrelson-esque twang and laconic countenance, Zada charms his 12 brethren by displaying Haymitch’s inherent empathy and kindness like a superpower. He’s able to calm those around him while growing increasingly incensed about the callous treatment foisted upon them. What Sunrise does best is purposefully remix the familiar tropes of the Games — mentor lessons, getting styled for camera, training for the arena — into a simmering thriller that connects the disenfranchised victors of the Games with secret sympathizers who are tired of Snow’s tyrannical grip on Panem.

Exposing the rot at the core of Snow’s regime distinguishes Sunrise from other chapters; this time around, Lawrence is surprisingly ruthless in portraying the Capitol’s enablers and sycophants. There’s no sentimentality extended to ghoulishly violent District 12 escort Drusilla Sickle (in a demented performance by Glenn Close) and her lavender marriage to stylist husband Magno Stift (Billy Porter). Even Elle Fanning’s capricious take on young Effie Trinket and Kieran Culkin’s coldly chaotic approach to Master of Ceremonies Caesar Flickerman are framed in a harsher light than Elizabeth Banks’ Effie or Stanley Tucci’s Caesar, and the film is better for it. Not even future rebellion architect and current Games producer Plutarch Heavensbee’s (Jesse Plemons) gets a pass for his sins of collusion, drawing a much stronger line in the sand about the evil Ralph Fiennes’ middle-aged Snow intentionally sows, and how complicit the Capitol residents are with their rapturous participation.

The arena isn’t just a backdrop but a puzzle to be solved as Haymitch embarks on a personal mission to cut the head off Snow’s showpiece. 

Visually, there’s much to admire about Uli Hanisch’s production design of the Quarter Quell arena and how beautifully cinematographer Jo Willems captures it. It’s like Ari Aster’s Midsommar had a baby with a Disney princess movie; the twisted landscape is a minefield of razor butterflies, rabid squirrels, and kamikaze birds for the tributes to survive. And much like Catching Fire, the arena isn’t just a backdrop but a puzzle to be solved as Haymitch embarks on a personal mission to cut the head off Snow’s showpiece.

Unlike The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, Sunrise is also long but paced more evenly, staying focused on Haymitch’s arc of defiance and then the heavy price he’s made to pay that eventually breaks him. Zada’s performance is so vulnerable and compelling that it ranks up there with Lawrence’s Katniss and Sutherland’s Snow in terms of indelible characterizations. Plemons is also terrific in portraying a more openly passionate Heavensbee who hasn’t yet learned to disappear from Snow’s eyeline.

In keeping with the hope that permeates Collins’ books and these films, Lawrence wraps up Sunrise by connecting it to the epilogue of Mockingjay – Part 2, and in doing so creates the rare full-circle cinematic moment that’s satisfying and appropriately feels like earned closure. Hopefully, the team (including Collins) sees it that way too, and they end the franchise here on a high note.

Across the arc of these six films, Collins, Jacobson, and Lawrence have successfully personalized the murky concept of authoritarianism, effectively warning younger generations how quickly ​​fascism can creep out of the pages of history and speculative science fiction into real life. And though The Hunger Games franchise is guilty of being too maximalist at times, there’s no denying the impact it’s had on popular culture — not only in memes, but in telling a satisfying allegory about the heartbreaking cost of war.

items.title: Elsinore Review
items.author: CarlosAMorales
items.content:
Another award season, another Shakespeare-adjacent film starring a well-liked actor who is apparently overdue for their state mandated awards campaign. Yes, since Jessie Buckley soared straight to an Oscar win last year for playing the Bard’s long-suffering wife Agnes in Chloé Zhao’s historical drama Hamnet, apparently it’s now time for another thespian to make a claim for the throne. This time it’s the ever-reliable Andrew Scott — an actor I’m never mad to see pop up in anything — working with director Simon Stone, who I’ve never had a strong opinion about one way or the other. The Swiss-born Australian filmmaker claims a for Shakespeare’s works, so it makes sense for him to jump at the chance to direct a movie about a man who would do anything to make his mark playing Hamlet before he dies. If only such passion had also managed to conjure up a good reason for the film to exist.

Elsinore, named for the castle where the events of the play Hamlet take place, stars Scott as Scottish actor Ian Charleson, an actor most famous for his work in 1981's Chariots of Fire and for later succumbing to AIDS after his National Theatre run as Hamlet in late 1989. The film dramatizes Charleson’s battle with the disease while under the care of Margaret Johnson (Olivia Colman), one of the UK’s earliest specialists in treating HIV/AIDS. Charleson’s drive to play the Prince of Denmark knowing he will most likely die in the process is as relatable and unerringly human as many of the dramatic impulses present in the play’s cast of characters. But the film’s construction — the pieces that are supposed to make it compelling as a visual story — short-change that emotional core more often than it can endure.

For a movie about a man dying of AIDS, Elsinore is far too blandly amiable. Charleson’s malaise with the results of his acting career and polite contempt for the smattering of fame he’s received are a good place to start, but he’s surrounded by too many good-natured and dramatically vacant supporting characters who basically exist to tell him he’s strong for toughing it out. Billie Piper is on hand as Patsy, Charleson’s token straight friend who offers him soup and smiles, and Johnny Flynn plays Richard Eyre, Charleson’s director who is only too understanding that his leading man may just collapse and die mid-performance. Even Colman’s Johnson, who routinely scolds Charleson for putting Hamlet ahead of his health, is tuned to more of an annoyance than an antagonist. Colman can trade barbs with the best of them, but there’s never any doubt that her Very Concerned resolve will ultimately melt in the face of Charleson’s peppy determination to make his eight o’clock curtain.

Elsinore may have a lot of drama on the stage, but it's severely lacking in such on the page.

The only person who actually challenges Charleson is Derek Jarman (David Dawson), the man who directed Charleson in the 1978 film, Jubilee. A fellow artist living with HIV, Jarman thinks Charleson is a sell-out for not living openly as a gay man and continuing to work with queer artists, and that Charleson’s desire for mainstream appeal is a disservice to the generation of gay men who are dropping like flies from the disease they share. Charleson’s rebuke that he doesn’t owe his life choices to anyone but himself, that he considers himself an actor more than an AIDS patient, is not only one of the film’s best scenes but also one of the only moments where Stephen Beresford’s screenplay depicts its subject as anything more than a summary. Elsinore may have a lot of drama on the stage, but it’s severely lacking in such on the page.

For his part, Scott is very good here. His precise but unfussy inhabitation of Charleson’s doomed conviviality is the number one reason to see Elsinore, and it will almost assuredly get him into the awards conversation as everyone involved intended. The way Scott manages to convey softly spoken but biting remarks as a critical point of character rather than an obtrusive affectation is commendable, as is his tenderness with the other patients that never belies false hope in their odds of survival. The scenes of Charleson rehearsing his lines and finding how he will channel his frustrations and anxieties into his performance as Hamlet are among the moments where the film really does come alive.

Sadly, Stone’s direction doesn’t do much to back Scott up. The flat colors and coherent but uninspired cinematography is all in service of not getting in the way of his actors’ legibility. It's a noble goal, but it makes the film anonymous on a formal level. Nor does it matter when the edit undermines Scott’s work; Stone chops up important scenes, including Charleson on the stage, as montages instead of letting them actually play out. I don’t understand why you would hire a lead actor with years of theater experience — including a run playing Hamlet — and not just let him Hamlet. That we don’t get five to ten uninterrupted minutes of just seeing Scott as Charleson giving his final performance — the one the movie has spent its whole runtime insisting is so important — is such a bizarre choice that I simply sat there confused as the credits rolled.

items.title: Daggerheart: Hope & Fear Expansion Review
items.author: Blythe Dujardin
items.content:
Critical Role’s TTRPG system, Daggerheart, puts a greater emphasis on story-telling than some of its peers. A year after the core book was released, Daggerheart offered players and Game Masters new options for telling their stories.with the system’s first expansion.

As someone who plays a variety of role-playing games on both sides of the GM screen, I’m always hungry for more options. More gear for my heroes to use and more vicious monsters to sic on my unsuspecting players.

Daggerheart: Hope and Fear adds a plethora of toys to the toybox, but if you weren’t a fan of the core book, don’t expect this expansion to change your mind.

Before diving into what’s new, for those unfamiliar, Daggerheart is a narrative-focused tabletop RPG system. It uses a rather handy card-based approach to help create and manage your characters and does away with the traditional initiative mechanic during combat. One of the most defining mechanics of Daggerheart, however, is its Hope and Fear dice.

These two twelve-sided dice, one representing your Hope value and the other Fear, can either cause your checks to earn you a 'Hope' resource that can be used to pull off extra special actions, or give your GM a 'Fear' point that they can spend. A proverbial "wrench in the gears" sort of treat, depending on which die rolls higher during the check. This mechanic also serves as the namesake for the system’s first expansion.

For players who have been wanting to make some new characters, a plethora of options await you inside this nearly 200-page tome. The Hope and Fear expansion comes with four new classes, each with two subclasses, six ancestries and communities, over 100 new pieces of gear and loot to dig through, and a brand-new domain. GMs get some new toys too, with 130+ new enemies to sic on those pesky heroes across 28 environments and four campaign frames (think of these as rough bases to build a campaign around). By far, though, my personal favorite inclusion in H&F is the brand-new Transformations system, but more on that gem in a bit.

The new domain, Dread, actually has some pretty interesting effects. The ones I found most intriguing and beneficial were abilities like Avatar of Terror, which makes you stronger the more Fear the GM has, and the spell Dire-Strike, which straight-up takes some of the GM’s Fear away. The idea that my friends and I could gang up and shut down the bullshit my GM might pull during a game instantly shot this new Domain to the top of my list for the next character I make.

"The idea that my friends and I could gang up and shut down the bullshit my GM might pull during a game instantly shot this new Domain to the top of my list for the next character I make."

Two new classes, the Assassin (a standalone, more stabby-focused rogue) and the Brawler (Daggerheart’s punchy monk-like class), utilize the core domains that came in the core book, while the other two new classes, the Warlock (make a pact with a thing, get cool powers) and the Witch (mess with enemies by hexing them), take advantage of H&F’s new Dread domain.

The new ancestries, which for D&D folks are basically Daggerheart’s equivalent to species, will feel familiar to anyone who’s played that other high-fantasy TTRPG. The Aetheris are winged, angel-y beings, while Elemental Kin—consisting of Earth, Ember (fire), Sky, and Tide (water) varieties—are individuals descended from powerful elementals. And then you have Gnomes, which are, well, gnomes.

All certainly good to have, but both the new ancestries and some of the new classes seem like such core fantasy staples that it feels odd to me that they weren’t included in the base release. Glad they’re here now, though, and gnomes being able to just teleport around with their Flicker Step feature is silly fun.

For the forever Game Masters out there (you are the real heroes), Hope & Fear’s new campaign frames offer good flexibility for running games for hesitant brand-new players or grizzled vets that want a challenge. My favorite out of the four offerings, surprisingly, is also the least complex: Castle High. Think modern-day wizard school where teenagers fly around on brooms while scrolling on their phones and take classes on giant floating islands in the sky. While I haven’t yet played or run the frame, the idea of swapping out my sword for pencil and paper and sneaking out of school instead of dungeons is a fun change of pace.

Of course, if you want to slay a dragon, or in this case a weredragon tyrant, you can do that too with Reign of the Weredragon. The most complex of the new offerings, Journey to Horizon, has you working to resurrect a goddess.

Now we can get to my favorite addition: transformations. Becoming a demigod, a werewolf, a vampire, or even living out your Danny Phantom dreams by transforming into a ghost is now possible! All of the transformation options in H&F (of which there are six) come with some sort of bonus or ability in addition to a downside. In Danny Phantom’s case, you take less physical damage but double magic damage, and can pass through solid objects at the cost of taking on some Stress.

I love transformations as a way to add further depth of your character or as a narrative plot thread, and the fact that they don’t count against any sort of domain or character limit (outside of only being allowed a single transformation at a time, but that’s what house rules are for) opens up all sorts of possibilities. Now, if Darrington Press could just make an official Super Sentai / Power Ranger transformation equivalent, I’d be all set! Castle High already features teenagers with attitude as the player characters, after all.

Daggerheart: Hope & Fear is a good first expansion, though it feels like a safe one. It adds a fair amount of new content for both players and GMs to mess around with, which is always great, even if some additions feel like they should have been included from the start. The Dread domain and how it can mess with the GM’s plans directly is a really fun twist. I’ve already gushed about the transformations, and I can’t wait to see what new options get added down the road.

That all said, since it launched, Daggerheart feels like a game that is far more intimidating to play for those who aren’t comfortable with improvisation and narrating what they are doing, and Hope & Fear doesn’t really help with that. I enjoy what it adds, but if you were already overwhelmed by the core game, don’t look to this expansion to save you. Daggerheart as a system is still, comparatively, in its infancy, and I would love to see a well-put-together starter kit or more hand-holdy expansion to help new players get into things.

items.title: Barbie Rewind Review
items.author: Rachel Weber
items.content:
Barbie Rewind feels like the equivalent of showing your children the family heirloom rocking horse, and then watching them poke it and ask if they can play Roblox. A weird mix of nostalgia and interior decorating sim, it's home to 17 retro Barbie games and a dreamhouse to arrange Barbie-appropriate furniture in. Now, it's been over three decades since I last smashed a Barbie against a G.I. Joe and made smooching noises, so I called in two gaming experts, Kora (9) and Paloma (5), to assist with this review. Sadly, unlike her looks, time has not been kind to Barbie's gaming legacy.

Why does she have a scuba mask but not a toilet?

"That doesn't make sense. Why does she have a scuba mask but not a toilet?" A crucial question from Kora as the girls got stuck into the only bit of Barbie Rewind they actually cared about: the decorating. This might be selling itself as a collection of Barbie games from 1991's NES Barbie through to 2007's Barbie as the Island Princess, but its newly created Dreamhouse mode is the big winner here. There are more than 250 pieces of furniture, and some of them are unlocked by playing the retro Barbie games. The big B and other characters like Ken and Christie give you quests, but they're just to decorate the house, so it's a bit like someone saying "be careful" when you're already falling down the stairs.

The Barbie games themselves got what I would call a polite fiddle. I played all of them before the expert advisors were called in, and Rewind is heavy on minigames of the platforming and "catch the falling coconut" variety. These games haven't been given the Monkey Island-style reboot; they're presented seemingly entirely as is, but with a frame that relates to their various consoles to help smooth over any aspect ratio issues.

It's great as a museum piece, but show it to anyone born after 2010 and they basically look like cave paintings. "Is that meant to be Barbie?" asks Kora incredulously, squinting at Barbie Pet Rescue. Paloma picks up the controller to play one of the minigames, a sort of cat Pong using two paws that is apparently essential to pet care, and watches the ball of yarn awkwardly bounce off the screen. She knows controllers, she plays Lego Batman, but this minigame makes no sense. The ball is slow, the angles are off, and Paloma looks at me exasperated as if I personally offended her.

Controls were an issue throughout, changing between games in a way that meant looking up the button layout for everything they wanted to try. One smart addition is the option to tweak things like your total health in certain games, which makes for a less stressful experience all round. The girls liked the concept of a lot of them – veterinarian duties, horse racing, and the fashion dress-up doll in particular – but these are kids born long after the time when you knew that what you saw on the cover of a game was light years away from how it actually looked. I could burn through pixelated bouncing and stilted dialogue on nostalgia alone, but Kora and Paloma are playing Hogwarts Legacy; they have iPad games, and their eyes know not the trauma of staring into a Gameboy Color in the back of a moving vehicle.

items.title: 12 12 12 Review
items.author: Leanne Butkovic
items.content:
This is a spoiler-free review of the first two episodes of , streaming on Apple TV now.

Apple TV’s 12 12 12 operates under these invented cardinal rules of a professional heist: It takes 12 months to plan, 12 hours to execute, and if the cops don’t catch the perpetrators in 12 days, they never will. (Why this didn’t premiere on December 12, I’ll never understand.) The series rests its entire weight on this premise, hopping between the three phases of a heist organized by Jamie Dornan’s Paul Galvin, a retired thief pulled back in for one last job, and the FBI agent relentlessly on his trail, Anthony Mackie’s Jack Strickland. The question is, then, does 12 12 12’s gimmick work? Based on the first two episodes, “I’m robbing the house on Christmas Eve while the family’s at mass” and “I Want My Halo Back,” the answer seems to be: not really.

12 12 12 starts with eyebrow-raising intrigue, as a crumpled, naked man slithers out of a lockbox inside a fancy-looking bank vault and starts cracking open safes. But the cutaway from this scene — right into the 12 12 12 explanation — is only the first instance of the main problem with the show thus far: switching over to a new window of time kills any of the momentum the previous scenes had going for them. 12 12 12 also approaches each of its nonlinear storylines with the same level of urgency. Hour 1 of Paul’s heist to steal the equivalent of one billion physical U.S. dollars — which, just how bulky is that in comparison, say, to the Breaking Bad storage unit stack? — from a Swiss bank moves with practically the same verve as Jack getting wise to what’s happened on the Day 1 hunt. It doesn’t help with differentiating either when both characters keep referencing “what happened in Newark” as the murky botched job from the past they won’t shut the hell up about nor actually explain beyond the obvious trauma they incurred from it.

12 12 12’s first two episodes, written by Dudi Appleton and Jim Keebble, treat that concept as though it’s that the audience could only follow the plot by spoon-feeding us time and place, and the script doubles down on this. The plot itself is full of cliches so that when it posits an occasionally unique idea it, by comparison, feels nearly revelatory. Of course, it often squanders that goodwill just as quickly. Just when you think 12 12 12 is going somewhere, its timeline triptych appears and swipes over to a new time period, resetting the action and deflating any of the excitement the show had just built. The dialogue is full of insufferable back-and-forths that are either inane or could have come from nearly any primetime cable procedural that’s attempting a quippy Marvel-ized punch-up.

Mackie and Dornan, two very competent actors, both make great efforts to do what they can with the trite material but to little avail. There’s only so much even accomplished actors can do with lines like “What if the only thing I’m good at is being a thief?” as Paul contemplates his girlfriend’s surprise pregnancy, or “You stole from me, Galvin. Now you’re gonna know how it feels,” as Jack promises to get revenge on Paul. For a show about pulling off the biggest bank heist in European history, it’s botched the job.

items.title: Heartland Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
Heartland is streaming on Netflix now.

A former country rock star searches for her missing niece in Shana Feste’s Heartland, a film with the broad appearance of a neo-noir, but one that doesn’t have nearly enough thrills or intrigue. The story comes from a place of love, both for country music and for Nashville. However, it unfolds too mechanically to unearth the seedy underbelly at which it hints, making for lackluster mystery despite Jessica Chastain’s enormous efforts at drawing emotions from a tepid script.

It begins interestingly enough, with Chastain’s washed-up, tough-as-nails musician Misty Jones huddled over a grave as she tearfully buries her dog before threatening the neighbor who killed it. None of this has any bearing on the larger plot, but it paints Misty as a cornered animal; she has nothing and no one. Her fridge is scant except for a forgotten Grammy she stores there for safe-keeping, a fun bit of environmental storytelling by way of visual information. Before long, though, this becomes the movie’s default lingua franca, with an unending number of shots of photographs and documents to try and piece together a whodunnit when Misty’s niece — the daughter of her estranged brother, an up-and-coming country artist named Charlie Heart (Carter Faith) — turns up missing.

This draws Misty back to the Nashville music scene, where she navigates ineffectual cops and seedy industry figures while retracing Charlie’s steps. The mystery of her disappearance runs parallel to Misty reacquainting herself with her problem-child past and through predatory people and places she once knew, leading to an eventual overlap of these simultaneous threads by way of a family secret. However, each time Heartland features a major reveal, it zips forward far too quickly alongside its umpteenth country music cue, as though it were entering some well-established final act.

In the process, what you’re left with is a story where Misty stumbles her way into information or ping-pongs between various characters — like Garett Hedlund’s charismatic producer Roy Combs — and ends up feeling like an inactive protagonist despite technically driving the plot. She moves from place to place, but rare are the moments when she puts two and two together. Chastain is remarkably locked-in as the aging country star — a woman who doesn’t want to be seen but is forced back into the spotlight. However, as convincing as her conception of Misty may be, it doesn’t matter all that much when every plot turn seems to fall into her lap.

This passive experience is further marred by mechanical filmmaking. While it all technically coheres — the nighttime spaces, lit by halogen signs, are all appropriately noxious; Feste manages to capture Chastain’s close-ups with clarity — you could practically set your watch by how each subplot plays out, and the way learning something new sends Misty charging to a new location at the end of practically every scene. It’s a languid film with no breathing room, an oxymoron that makes sense once the film winds up and you can recount how much has happened by way of plot, and how little by way of story or emotional development. For instance, there are hints and flashbacks about her ex-husband and musical partner Clark (John Hawkes) throughout, but his appearance is relegated to late in the runtime while his actual role as a specter of her past ends up with little actual impact.

Its country music interludes play like wheel-spinning interruptions despite gesturing at phantom connections between violence and the genre at large.

The pieces for some other more rigorous story all appear to be in place, from people Misty knows she can’t trust to former friends with whom she needs to make amends. Unfortunately, Heartland strings these together in rote fashion. Its camera is used to tell more than to show, and its country music interludes play like wheel-spinning interruptions despite gesturing at phantom connections between violence and the genre at large. The film, as a whole, feels episodic and disconnected.

Through it all, Chastain remains remarkable as ever; unfortunately, it’s as a woman who would rather be anywhere else — a feeling that’s hard to shake when sitting down to watch Heartland for yourself.

items.title: Yaga Episode 5 Recap and Review
items.author: Jessie Wade
items.content:
Warning: This review contains full spoilers for Season 1, Episode 5. Episodes 1-5 are now streaming on AMC+ in the US and Crave in Canada, with new episodes releasing on Fridays at midnight PT.

Following up on Episode 4’s chaotic and eventful ending, Episode 5 gives us the most reveals we’ve seen yet in Yaga. Picking up right where we left, we find out Laney is not in fact dead, but instead went into cardiac arrest – with a pissed off Eckert yelling at both Carson and Rapp for being the cause of it.

Rapp explains his theory as to what is happening in this town, which includes Laney thinking she is Baba Yaga and luring people such as Henry, Logan, Angel, and others into her chicken hut in the woods for manifestation rituals and sacrifices.

As they go their separate ways, we find out more unhinged details involving this mystery. Rapp ends up seeing a little girl (who very well may be a vision) who echoes what Laney said in the hospital – that Henry is a “bad dog” and is in Baba Yaga’s chicken house. Immediately after, Rapp finds a mysterious package in his rental car, and upon opening it, he finds a carved box with chicken feathers and what looks to be Henry’s phone. The sinister mask is set as the phone’s background and there’s a raw audio recording for him to play of the podcast episode Henry did with Katherine, which unfolds into fascinating revelations.

On the other side of things, Carson and Eckert are trying to track down who uploaded the video of Logan’s body by speaking to various people around town. One of the familiar faces is Katherine, who throughout the episode (and the show overall) seems to constantly drop suspicious clues, almost too casually, for it to not be intentional.

From mentioning the diner owner, Geena, cooking the chickens who stop laying eggs, to telling Carson she and Rapp “look good together” while giving her a sly look, to bumping into Eckert and seeing images of the mask, telling him she loves the artist’s work, Katherine seems to be dropping information right into their laps. And in this episode, it’s more apparent than it’s ever been.

As Rapp continues on his search in the woods, we see Katherine in her office with Henry recording the podcast, and surprisingly, Logan is there to manage the tech of it all. This is the first time we get to really see Hudson Williams at length as Henry, and his portrayal of the billionaire playboy is chilling while he tries to charm Katherine with his outright crude methods.

It’s pretty apparent that Henry is trying to get information on Baba Yaga for some reason, as he inquires about witches eating bones and casually mentions the retreat he attends – all with an obvious underlying sexual interest in Katherine.

Carrie-Anne Moss as Katherine absolutely owns this episode with her incredible storytelling and her ability to bewitch anyone in her orbit. By the end of the podcast (and the episode as a whole) you’re left wondering who actually seduced who into their bed? Who holds the power of the seduction?

The theme of men being inappropriate and downright sexually assaulting women in this show rears its ugly head yet again, with Henry having deliberately brushed his hand against Katherine’s breast without consent, and Eckert kissing Carson while they were at his house working on the case. In the latter scene, she shoves him off of her and he comments, “it’s not like I was trying to fuck you.” It’s a disturbing but accurate reality for many people and the show bringing this theme to light is as important as it is difficult to watch.

“Women? We’re angry about everything.”

As night comes – and right when we think Rapp is actually focusing on being responsible – he makes his way over to Katherine’s house, surprising her. Yet she invites him in for dinner. While they discuss the podcast and details from it that Rapp is trying to get answers on, Katherine continues her casual attitude and shares how she relates to Baba Yaga. “She resonates with me, with women. She’s a figure of great power, wisdom, rage.” Rapp asks her if she’s angry about something, to which Katherine responds, “Women? We’re angry about everything.” Any woman watching this scene will likely relate to the safe door Moss just opened with the perfection that is that line.

Towards the end of the episode, we can sense how intoxicating the sexual tension is that has built up between Katherine and Rapp as, filled with passion and lust, they grab each other to have sex on her living room floor. On the opposite side of things, we get confirmation of Carson’s feelings for Rapp as she’s at her place, rightfully upset over her assault and that Rapp wouldn’t respond to her texts, as we see her sniff his tank top in her hands while pleasuring herself in the same moments Rapp and Katherine are having sex.

After they finish, we see Rapp looking at his reflection in the bathroom mirror – taking in the nail and bite marks and other bruises – when a vision seems to flicker through. Henry’s standing next to him, puts his hand around his throat and pulls him in for a brutal kiss. All of a sudden, Henry looks into the mirror, opens his mouth, and screams as blood pours out of it.

In that moment, the scene stops and jumps to Rapp jolting and standing in the hallway as he hears someone scream and pound on Katherine’s front door. He looks toward the clock on the wall, seeing the time flip to 3:33, and then sees Geena’s daughter, Lily, at the door. She starts throwing up blood as Katherine runs to grab her, while Rapp finds a tooth on the ground and holds it up in curiosity.

We’re now left with more questions than we started in this episode, including finding out Henry bought three of the creepy witch masks from the artist, while Rapp discovered a large triskele symbol made out of moss in the middle of the woods – which seems to be the circle Laney uses for her retreats. We also find out Katherine gifted Henry the Aztec knife that was allegedly the murder weapon for Logan, while lying smoothly to Rapp about it. Who do we think is behind all of this? Is there one true Baba Yaga or is it a cult of culprits?

items.title: Ebenezer Review
items.author: Tom Jorgensen
items.content:
One need only look to The Muppet Christmas Carol, the best Christmas movie of them all, to understand why Charles Dickens’ novella has endured countless adaptations over the nearly two hundred years since it was published. The miserly Ebenezer Scrooge’s confrontation with the ghosts of his past with hopes for a brighter future is so fundamentally strong that a staging of it by Michael Caine and Kermit the Frog that blends all sorts of tones and meta commentary has room not only to work, but to stand as an unambiguously respected adaptation of the text. Ti West’s Ebenezer feels most focused on illuminating the darker corners of Dickens’ tale, but the broad and classically Johnny Depp performance at its heart holds it back from ever elevating into a more meaningful adaptation of the text.

A Christmas Carol is, of course, a ghost story at its heart, and Ti West’s long history in the horror genre - including a ghost story of his own, The Innkeepers - makes him an interesting director to see paired with the material. West’s instincts on how and where to amp up A Christmas Carol’s spooky trappings are strong from the top down, and they’re most evident in Ebenezer’s production design. Ebenezer leans on the austere chill of its Victorian London setting well with practical sets and stages that instantly read as Christmas Carol-appropriate. The destitute and dour look of the film illuminates both the poverty Scrooge hates and the corresponding spiritual bankruptcy from which he suffers in equal measure. Tyler Bates’ string-heavy score helps to push that sense of unease, with the highlight piece being a driving and ominous string quartet version of “Carol of the Bells” played over the opening credits of Londoners bringing out decorations and getting ready for the approaching holiday.

While Ebenezer is largely a faithful adaptation of Dickens’ novella, West and writer Nathaniel Halpern embellish certain turns of the plot to underscore either Scrooge’s inner turmoil or the story’s horror elements, like adding a new prologue featuring Scrooge’s business partner Jacob Marley (Ian McKellen). The prologue serves the dual purpose of starting West’s darker take on the story off with a body (“Marley wasdead: to begin with,” and all that) and giving McKellen just a little bit more time on camera. Formative events like Ebenezer’s tough childhood or his failed engagement with Belle get expounded on with enough care to work on their own merits, but with Depp’s Ebenezer tough to connect to emotionally, little of the new additions wind up feeling impactful enough to justify the time spent on them. Despite coming in just under two hours, each of the “staves” that Ebenezer is chaptered into routinely taper off in momentum before West is moving on to the next act of the story.

A director’s influence can only take Ebenezer Scrooge’s story so far. Any staging of A Christmas Carol lives and dies on the casting of its Scrooge: the whole story is told over Scrooge’s shoulder, and whatever catharsis the audience is able to experience through Scrooge’s own as he wakes up on Christmas Day a changed man has to be channeled through an accessible and readably human performance. That leaves Johnny Depp’s work here as Ebenezer Scrooge feeling like a frustrating misfire.
